items.text: Maldives police said two Maldivian Flydubai co-pilots held in the UAE in connection with the FZ1073 investigation were sent home Friday and are being questioned.
items.detail: Maldives Police Service spokesperson Ahmed Shiyam said the two pilots arrived in the Maldives on Friday morning and officers met them at Velana International Airport to question them and clarify information about the Sept. 30 incident. He said they have not been arrested and that police will announce any decision to take action against them. Neither the UAE nor the Maldives has said what role, if any, the two had. The UAE attorney general has said the Omani co-pilot confessed and claimed he acted alone, while investigators keep checking for accomplices or other links. No charges have been announced in the case.
items.why: It is the first official word that the investigation has reached other Flydubai pilots, though no link to the plot has been established.

items.source: Bend Police Department; Bend-La Pine Schools; AP
items.text: A 16-year-old shooter killed three children and a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday, police said; the shooter is dead.
items.detail: The shooting happened about 1 p.m. PT (4 p.m. ET) Thursday. Bend police said they got a call at 12:59 p.m. PT about a person shooting into a car outside Silver Rail Elementary, followed about a minute later by multiple 911 calls reporting that the person had entered the school and opened fire. Officers arrived at 1:02 p.m. and the shooter was down seconds later, police said. Police said the attacker forced his way in by shooting at locked doors and was shot by a person at the scene who pursued him into the school; he was found dead inside minutes after the first report. Police Chief Mike Krantz said the children killed were ages 5, 8 and 11. A 7-year-old child and a teacher were taken to the hospital in critical condition. The shooter's identity has not been released. Bend-La Pine Schools canceled classes and athletic events districtwide for Friday.
items.why: It is one of the deadliest U.S. elementary school shootings in years, and officials are still investigating how it unfolded.

items.text: Wholesale prices jumped 1.3% in September, the biggest monthly rise since March 2022, while retail sales rose 0.8% on pricier gas.
items.detail: The Bureau of Labor Statistics said its final-demand Producer Price Index rose 1.3% in September after 0.5% in August, and is up 6.3% over 12 months, the most since December 2022. Goods prices rose 2.6%, the largest increase since the series began in 2009; energy rose 10.8% and gasoline 20.3%. Services rose 0.8%. Separately, the Census Bureau's advance estimate put September retail sales at $745.0 billion, up 0.8% from August and 6.3% from a year earlier; August was revised up to 1.3%. Gas station sales rose 6.4% for the month, and sales excluding gas stations rose just 0.2%.
items.why: A day after 3.7% consumer inflation, the fastest wholesale price gains since 2022 point to more price pressure ahead.
items.source: Bureau of Labor Statistics (PPI release); Census Bureau (retail sales)

items.text: The Dow closed up about 1.1%, more than 500 points, Thursday as investors moved money out of tech stocks and into Treasury bonds.
items.detail: The S&P 500 rose 0.3% and the Nasdaq 0.1% after recovering from an intraday drop of more than 1%; the S&P tech sector fell 0.5%. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to about 5.09%, its biggest one-day drop since Aug. 1, the Wall Street Journal reported. Nike, Home Depot and Sherwin-Williams led the Dow. The moves followed the hotter-than-expected wholesale price report and Wednesday's worst day since July for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq.
items.why: Money left AI-linked stocks for bonds and consumer companies as investors weighed what hotter inflation means for interest rates.

items.text: The International Energy Agency's members agreed to speed up release of their remaining 100 million barrels of emergency oil, including over 20 million barrels of diesel.
items.detail: The IEA Governing Board said about 330 million barrels have been released so far under the March 2026 collective action responding to the Strait of Hormuz crisis. Members agreed to accelerate the remaining roughly 100 million barrels, with more than 20 million barrels of diesel to go out as soon as possible, bringing total releases above the original 400 million barrels. The board cited continued tight oil markets, especially for diesel, and urged producers to raise output.
items.why: Diesel led September's price spike, and this is the main coordinated effort to add supply.

items.text: Iraq's International Development Bank and two Iranian offshore banks were sanctioned by Treasury for allegedly giving Iran access to U.S. dollars.
items.detail: The designations, under Operation Economic Outcast and Executive Order 13902, also cover Iranian offshore banks Jazireh International Bank and Chabahar International Bank Overseas, Dubai-based oil intermediary Sayyed Ruhollah Razavi and two of his companies, Hong Kong's Elitesphere Trading, and four Iranian exchange houses and their owners. The State Department separately designated Cuba's Banco Internacional de Comercio for serving Iran's Karafarin Bank. Their U.S. assets are blocked, and foreign banks dealing with them risk secondary sanctions. Treasury's FinCEN also issued an alert asking banks to flag possible Iranian abuse of religious charities.
items.why: It is the latest round in Washington's campaign to cut off Iran's remaining financial lifelines during the war.
items.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury (press release)

items.text: Yemen's presidential palace in Aden, seat of the internationally recognized government, was hit by Houthi missiles, killing at least two people.
items.detail: Officials first said two security personnel were killed when ballistic missiles struck al-Maashiq Palace; Yemen's health minister later put the toll at five dead and 16 injured. The information minister told the BBC the prime minister and other ministers were not hurt. Houthi spokesman Yahya Sarea said the group struck what it called the Saudi military's operations headquarters in Aden. Saudi Arabia's deputy foreign minister accused Iran of encouraging the Houthi escalation.
items.why: The Houthi fight with Saudi Arabia has reached a direct strike on the Yemeni government's seat.

items.court: Ohio Tenth District Court of Appeals
items.text: Ohio's EdChoice private-school voucher program is unconstitutional, a state appeals court ruled, though vouchers continue while the state appeals.
items.detail: A three-judge panel of the Tenth District Court of Appeals ruled 3-0 in Columbus City School District v. State of Ohio, upholding a Franklin County trial court that found EdChoice funds a separate school system in conflict with the Ohio Constitution. The court kept enforcement on hold pending an expected appeal. About 180,000 students use EdChoice, which became universal in 2023. Attorney General Andy Wilson said the state will appeal to the Ohio Supreme Court and that there is no immediate impact on families.
items.why: One of the country's largest voucher programs now heads to the Ohio Supreme Court.
items.source: Ohio Tenth District Court of Appeals (decision)

items.court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York
items.text: Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela's ousted leader, had a not-guilty plea entered for him in New York federal court on new torture-conspiracy charges.
items.detail: Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, were arraigned on a superseding indictment filed last week charging them with conspiracy to commit torture. Maduro called the charges false before Judge Alvin Hellerstein cut him off and entered the plea; Flores pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors say the couple ran a violent system of repression under which thousands of Venezuelans, including U.S. citizens, were killed, harassed or tortured. The new count adds to earlier narco-terrorism, cocaine-trafficking and weapons charges. The couple were captured in a U.S. military raid in January; trial is set for June 2027.
items.why: A former foreign head of state now faces torture charges in a U.S. courtroom.

items.text: Two chemical tankers off Romania's Black Sea coast were hit by drones, Romania's president said, and seven of one ship's 12 crew are missing.
items.detail: The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader reported blasts and a fire around 7 a.m. local time Thursday about 13 nautical miles off Sulina, at the mouth of the Danube. President Nicușor Dan said it and the Comoros-flagged Yara J, hit Wednesday with its crew safe, were both struck by drones. Helicopters and rescue boats are searching in high waves. Romania's and Bulgaria's leaders were set to discuss whether to request NATO consultations under Article 4, and Dan was due to meet NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels. Russia said it hit two cargo ships carrying military cargo to Odesa but did not name them.
items.why: Drone strikes on ships in a NATO member's waters left crew missing and put alliance consultations on the table.

items.text: Cornell's Faculty Senate began debating a no-confidence resolution in the university's administration over its handling of the Jane Doe case.
items.detail: At a Wednesday meeting closed to the media, President Michael Kotlikoff took faculty questions before the debate, acknowledged some missteps and asked for more time to carry out reforms, according to an audio recording obtained by the Associated Press. He said that if Cornell cannot be convinced fraternities can operate safely, it should make that decision, based on research and evidence. He also said he had not read the Cornell Police report on the 2024 allegations, citing confidentiality and policy. Debate resumes Oct. 28, followed by electronic voting; the nonbinding resolution cannot remove him. Attorney General Letitia James's criminal investigation continues; no one has been criminally charged, and the men named in the civil lawsuit deny the accusations.
items.why: Cornell's faculty will formally vote on whether they trust the administration, and the president has now left open ending fraternity life.

items.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar's phone was seized by federal authorities, who also issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to her relatives, in a criminal probe.
items.detail: The phone was taken during the search of the Minnesota Democrat's Washington home, AP reported Oct. 14, citing a person familiar with the case. The subpoenas are for a Minnesota grand jury looking into possible false statements in immigration paperwork, AP, MPR News and CBS News reported; Omar herself was not subpoenaed. No charges have been announced.
items.why: A sitting member of Congress is the subject of a federal criminal investigation weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms.

items.text: Spanish ships would pay a $200,000 fee for every voyage to U.S. ports under a Federal Maritime Commission proposal that also limits some Spanish imports.
items.detail: The proposed rule, published in the Federal Register Oct. 15, responds to what the commission calls unfavorable shipping conditions created by Spain's government denying vessels entry to Spanish ports. It would also restrict imports of certain Spanish goods. Nothing takes effect yet: comments are open until Dec. 14, and the commission is offering a public hearing.
items.why: It is a rare U.S. shipping penalty aimed at a European ally and could raise costs on Spanish goods.
items.source: Federal Register (Federal Maritime Commission proposed rule)

items.text: Airlines' new, more detailed reporting on why flights are delayed or canceled was pushed back to Feb. 1, 2027, by the Transportation Department.
items.detail: A final rule published Oct. 15 delays the department's Sept. 3 rule setting new delay and cancellation cause categories required by the 2024 FAA Reauthorization Act. Airlines for America asked for the delay, saying the Bureau of Transportation Statistics needed time to update its reporting instructions.
items.why: Travelers will wait longer for clearer public data on what causes flight delays and cancellations.

items.text: The FCC does not have to rule within 48 hours on Democratic candidates' challenge to cheaper campaign ad rates for party committees, the Supreme Court said.
items.detail: In an unsigned opinion Oct. 14 in FCC v. Brown (26A476), the Court stayed an Oct. 7 Fourth Circuit order that gave the FCC until Oct. 9 to decide the candidates' application, saying the Communications Act sets no deadline and the appeals court could not force the agency to cut short its process. The FCC's March notice saying parties engaged in coordinated activity get the law's lowest ad rates stays in place; the Court had already put the Fourth Circuit's earlier ruling on hold Sept. 4. Justices Sotomayor and Jackson would have denied the stay.
items.why: Party committees keep access to the lowest TV ad rates in the final weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms.
items.source: Supreme Court of the United States (opinion)

items.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
items.text: California's law requiring plainclothes federal agents to show identification cannot be enforced against them, a federal appeals court ruled.
items.detail: A Ninth Circuit panel (Judges Nguyen, Bennett and Collins) on Oct. 14 reversed a district judge and ordered a preliminary injunction barring California, Gov. Gavin Newsom and Attorney General Rob Bonta from enforcing Section 10 of the No Vigilantes Act against federal agencies and officers. That section requires non-uniformed federal officers working in California to visibly display ID, with criminal penalties for violators. The court said the Justice Department is likely to win its claim that the state cannot directly regulate how federal officers do their jobs under the Constitution's Supremacy Clause.
items.why: It lets federal immigration and other agents keep working in California without displaying ID while the case continues.
items.source: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (opinion)

items.court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York
items.text: The court ban on taxpayer-funded TV ads promoting President Trump was extended to Nov. 8 after more than 30 ads aired despite the judge's halt order.
items.detail: U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon extended her Oct. 11 temporary restraining order by two weeks, allowed Common Cause fast-tracked discovery into who paid for the ads and why they kept running over the Columbus Day holiday, and set arguments on a preliminary injunction for Nov. 4. A federal prosecutor apologized in court Wednesday, saying he failed to make sure the agency complied on Sunday night. The roughly $20 million DHS campaign ran on cable news and football telecasts.
items.why: The ads stay off the air through the Nov. 3 midterms, and the court is now probing why its order was not followed.

items.text: Yes-or-no options betting on company numbers like quarterly revenue can now be listed on a U.S. stock-options exchange after SEC approval.
items.detail: The SEC voted Oct. 13 to approve Cboe's rule change allowing cash-settled binary options tied to key performance indicators that certain listed companies report. Chairman Paul Atkins said the contracts will trade under the same exchange rules and investor protections as existing options, and that the order does not decide CFTC jurisdiction over similar contracts built differently.
items.why: It brings prediction-market-style bets on company results onto a regulated securities exchange.

items.text: Russia fired 580 drones and two missiles at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine's Air Force said, killing three people in the Kirovohrad region.
items.detail: The Air Force said 536 drones were shot down or jammed as of 8 a.m. local time Thursday, with hits at 31 locations and falling debris at 11 more; the two Kh-59 missiles were fired from the Black Sea. The figures were preliminary and the attack was still under way when they were released. AP reported the three deaths in Kirovohrad, the hardest-hit region.
items.why: It is one of the largest drone barrages in weeks, days after an announced energy truce.
items.source: Ukrainian Air Force via Hromadske; AP

items.text: Ukraine resumed drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, setting Rosneft's Ryazan refinery on fire in its first energy strike since President Trump's announced truce.
items.detail: Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov said a large drone attack caused a fire at the refinery, which handles almost 5% of Russia's refining and supplies fuel to Moscow. President Zelenskyy told the Financial Times that Ukraine paused energy strikes for three days at U.S. request but would resume because Russia kept hitting Ukraine's power grid. Russia's defense ministry said debris from downed drones caused the fire.
items.why: It ends the short U.S.-requested pause on strikes against energy sites.

items.text: Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran was hit in a Houthi strike that damaged the offices of the oil giant's chief executive and other top officials.
items.detail: Two regional officials told AP the strike targeted the top three floors of a building used by senior executives, with no casualties. New explosions were also heard in Riyadh on Wednesday, again blamed on Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis. Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guard navy said a cargo ship carrying 2,500 containers sank after hitting a mine in the Strait of Hormuz; AP could not verify it.
items.why: A strike on the world's largest oil company's headquarters adds to the risk to Gulf energy supplies.

items.text: TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker, said third-quarter profit jumped 69% to a record T$763.1 billion (about $23.6 billion) on AI chip demand.
items.detail: The result for July through September beat the T$746.3 billion LSEG SmartEstimate, Reuters reported. TSMC makes chips for Nvidia and Apple, and its results are closely watched as a read on spending for AI hardware.
items.why: TSMC's numbers show whether the AI chip boom behind big tech stocks is still growing.

items.text: A school roof collapse in Peshawar, Pakistan, killed at least 28 children and a teacher and injured more than 50, AP reported.
items.detail: The roof fell at the private Al-Khair school in northwestern Pakistan on Thursday. A Lady Reading Hospital spokesman said all the children killed or hurt were 13 or younger. Rescuers were still searching the rubble, and the toll could rise.
items.why: Dozens of young children were killed when a single school building failed.

items.court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California
items.text: The State Department must open the 2027 diversity visa lottery, which it had skipped this year, a federal judge ordered.
items.detail: U.S. District Judge Jinsook Ohta in San Diego granted a preliminary injunction Oct. 14 in Red Eagle Law v. Rubio. She ordered Secretary of State Marco Rubio to publicly announce the DV-2027 registration period, including dates, the entry website and requirements, by midnight Oct. 15, including in the Federal Register, and to keep registration open for 30 days. The department must accept eligible electronic entries, notify those selected and process applications until the visas run out or the fiscal year ends Sept. 30, 2027. The program offers up to 55,000 green cards a year; the administration had not opened registration on time and argued it was too late.
items.why: Up to 55,000 green cards for 2027 are back in play after the program had effectively been canceled.
items.source: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California (order, via Courthouse News)

items.court: U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California
items.text: The Agriculture Department must halt its reorganization, including forced moves of about 2,600 Washington-area employees, a federal judge ordered.
items.detail: U.S. District Judge Vince Chhabria granted federal unions' stay request Oct. 13, finding USDA had "almost certainly" used congressionally appropriated money for office closures and relocations in violation of a spending-law ban on reorganizing without congressional approval. USDA must stop issuing or enforcing reassignment letters, tell employees within two days and confirm compliance within a week. The order also protects the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center in Maryland, which the plan would have closed. The judge said relief may be short because the restriction is in the stopgap funding law that expires Dec. 11.
items.why: Thousands of USDA workers facing move-or-quit orders get a reprieve at least until Congress revisits the funding restriction.

items.text: Affordable Care Act premium tax credits would be limited to citizens, nationals and certain lawfully present noncitizens starting in 2027 under proposed Treasury and IRS rules.
items.detail: Treasury and the IRS issued proposed regulations Oct. 14 putting into effect the Premium Tax Credit changes in the Working Families Tax Cuts law. Beginning in 2027 they restrict eligibility, apply eligibility checks and add new verification requirements for advance credit payments. HHS is expected to issue parallel proposed rules on exchange procedures.
items.why: It sets who can get federal help paying for marketplace health insurance starting in 2027.

items.text: Consumer prices rose 3.7% over the past year in September, up from 3.4% in August, as gasoline jumped 9.1% in a month.
items.detail: The Bureau of Labor Statistics said its consumer price index rose 0.6% in September after 0.4% in August, with gasoline accounting for over half of the monthly gain. Prices excluding food and energy rose 0.3% for the month and 2.6% over the year (2.4% in August). Energy prices are up 20.4% over 12 months and gasoline 34.2%; food was unchanged for the month. Stocks had their worst day since July: the S&P 500 fell 1.1%, the Nasdaq 1.9% and the Dow 0.1%, AP reported. The October report is due Nov. 10.
items.why: Faster inflation squeezes household budgets and raises the odds the Fed lifts rates again at its Oct. 27-28 meeting.

items.text: A Singapore-flagged container ship, GFS Pride, sank in the Strait of Hormuz after an unknown projectile hit it, Singapore said; all 21 crew got off safely.
items.detail: Singapore's Maritime and Port Authority said GFS Pride was struck Tuesday, caught fire and sank; no injuries were reported. A second Singapore-flagged container ship, GFS Giselle, took hull damage from a projectile Wednesday but reached a safe anchorage with all 22 crew. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines while using what they called an "unauthorised" route. The only other ship reported sunk since the Iran war began in February was the Safeen Prestige in March; the UN's maritime agency counts at least 24 seafarers killed in 106 confirmed incidents.
items.why: A sinking in the strait that carries about a fifth of the world's oil and gas raises the risk for every ship still moving Gulf exports.
items.source: BBC (citing Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore)

items.text: Bank of America's third-quarter profit fell 17% to $6.9 billion after a $1.2 billion federal penalty, while Morgan Stanley's profit rose to $4.9 billion.
items.detail: Bank of America earned 91 cents a share; excluding the penalty for anti-money-laundering and sanctions failures, it would have been $1.08. Revenue rose 3.2% to $30.1 billion but missed estimates as bond trading revenue fell 17% to $2.55 billion, CNBC reported; net interest income rose 7.9% to $16.6 billion. Morgan Stanley reported net revenue of $20.3 billion, up from $18.2 billion a year earlier, and earnings of $3.03 a share, with $232 billion in net new wealth-management assets.
items.why: The second day of big-bank results showed trading slowing at one of the largest U.S. lenders as a record penalty hit its books.
items.source: Bank of America (Q3 2026 results, SEC filing)

items.text: The Justice Department's first national tax fraud surge brought cases against 76 defendants accused of trying to take more than $490 million from the Treasury.
items.detail: DOJ's new Fraud Division, 35 U.S. attorney's offices and IRS Criminal Investigation ran the surge from early September to Oct. 14. Prosecutors brought 23 actions with new charges against 31 defendants, with an alleged intended loss above $350 million, plus about 39 trials, guilty pleas and sentencings involving 45 others (nearly $140 million). The largest case charges four Texas residents with selling a sham-trust tax shelter that allegedly hid more than $1.5 billion of income and cost the IRS over $200 million. Charges are allegations; defendants are presumed innocent.
items.why: It is the first coordinated nationwide criminal tax sweep under the Fraud Division created in April.

items.text: The Fed's Beige Book found most of its 12 districts saw little change in consumer spending, with spending driven by high-income households.
items.detail: Two districts reported moderate growth, three modest, four slight and three no significant change since the prior report. Robust manufacturing growth led Dallas, and six other districts reported modest to moderate factory growth. Most districts reported little or no net change in employment. Auto sales were flat to lower in five of six districts that reported, and Boston, Minneapolis and San Francisco noted fewer Canadian tourists. Information was collected on or before Oct. 5; the report feeds into the Fed's Oct. 27-28 rate meeting.
items.why: It is the Fed's last broad read on the economy before a rate meeting where a hike is in play.

items.text: A Russian drone strike killed six people and injured 13, including a child, in Lutsk in western Ukraine, Ukraine's emergency service said.
items.detail: The State Emergency Service said search and rescue work was finished and one injured person was in critical condition. Drone debris hit a wholesale warehouse, and a nine-story apartment building on Sobornosti Avenue was damaged, officials said. The strike came hours after an overnight Russian attack that cut power to at least 600,000 Ukrainians despite the energy ceasefire Trump announced Sunday.
items.why: Deadly strikes are reaching far western Ukraine even as Washington presses an energy truce.

items.text: Russian missiles and drones knocked out power to at least 600,000 Ukrainians overnight, killing three in Kyiv, three days after Trump's announced energy ceasefire.
items.detail: Zelenskyy said the hours-long attack, aimed mainly at Kyiv and Kharkiv, damaged 30 energy facilities and called it "ostentatious disrespect" to President Trump's peace effort. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 39 ballistic and cruise missiles and 128 drones. Russia's defense ministry said it struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, plus other targets, and attacks also hit state railway facilities in five regions. Trump announced the energy ceasefire on Sunday; Zelenskyy says Ukraine has held off strikes on Russian refineries since then.
items.why: It is the largest blow yet to the energy truce Washington announced, heading into Ukraine's heating season.

items.text: CNN, MS NOW and Politico keep their White House access for the rest of their lawsuit after a federal judge blocked President Trump's ban late Tuesday.
items.detail: U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly in Washington issued a preliminary injunction, replacing the temporary restraining order he granted Sept. 24, and found the outlets likely to win their free-speech and due-process claims. He wrote that Trump likely banned them because he sees their reporting as biased, and noted the national-security reason came after their passes were pulled. The order has no end date but does not require access to the Oval Office or Air Force One. It is not a final ruling on the merits.
items.why: It keeps three major outlets inside the White House while the court decides whether a president can bar reporters over their coverage.

items.text: The Trump administration's rule for fining migrants up to $998 a day for not leaving the U.S. was made final today, after a Boston judge stayed the earlier version.
items.detail: Homeland Security and the Justice Department finalized the June 2025 interim rule with one change: ICE may accept a late appeal when a documented mail delay was beyond the person's control. Appeals are still due within 15 business days. The rule covers fines for failing to leave after a final removal order (up to $998 a day), missing a voluntary-departure deadline and being caught entering illegally. A federal judge in Massachusetts stayed the interim rule and the fines issued under it, finding ICE likely skipped required public comment; the departments say that stay does not stop the final rule from taking effect immediately. DHS also proposed today to end the rule telling USCIS officers to defer to earlier approvals when deciding H-1B, L-1, O-1 and other work-visa extensions; comments are due Nov. 13.
items.why: The administration is trying to restart more than 100,000 fines worth about $84 billion that a court had halted.

items.text: ASML, the sole maker of the machines that print advanced AI chips, said its planned supply for 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet customer demand.
items.detail: The Dutch company reported record third-quarter sales of 11.7 billion euros and net income of 5.0 billion euros, up from 9.3 billion and 2.9 billion in the second quarter, with a 57.5% gross margin. It expects fourth-quarter sales of 14.2 billion to 15.2 billion euros and full-year 2026 sales of 44 billion to 45 billion euros. CEO Christophe Fouquet said some customers want to place orders for 2029 and 2030, and ASML is studying ways to add capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase it announced earlier.
items.why: A shortage of ASML machines caps how fast chipmakers can expand AI chip output.

items.text: The Supreme Court agreed to decide whether DOGE must turn over records to a watchdog group under the public-records law.
items.detail: In U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (No. 25-1103), the justices granted the Trump administration's appeal in Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington's Freedom of Information Act case. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled in April 2025 that DOGE likely is an agency covered by FOIA; the administration says DOGE is an advisory body inside the Executive Office of the President and exempt. The Supreme Court in June 2025 ordered the D.C. Circuit to narrow the judge's discovery orders; the D.C. Circuit refused in July to halt the narrowed disclosure. Arguments are expected early in 2027, with a ruling by summer. The court also agreed to hear Blanche v. Ozurumba (No. 25-1343), on whether cooking at a Nigerian separatist group's camp counts as "material support" for terrorism that bars an immigrant from asylum.
items.why: The case will decide how much of the White House's cost-cutting operation the public can see, and sets a test for other EOP offices.
items.source: Supreme Court of the United States (order list)

items.text: Bank of America was hit with more than $1.21 billion in federal penalties for anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, Treasury said.
items.detail: Treasury called it the third-largest penalty in its history. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's $750 million civil penalty, credited toward the total, is the largest the OCC has ever imposed. In its resolution with FinCEN, the bank admitted it willfully violated the Bank Secrecy Act; Treasury said it failed to report on time more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, over $1 billion of it tied to national-security risks such as Chinese money-laundering networks and the southwest border. The bank must hire a third party to find unreported transactions and undergo independent reviews. OFAC separately announced an $11.66 million settlement over 475 apparent sanctions violations. The bank said the penalties mean a $1.2 billion third-quarter charge; it reports earnings Wednesday.
items.why: A record OCC penalty against the second-largest U.S. bank, the day before its earnings.

items.text: Homeland Security made final its end to automatic work-permit extensions for immigrants awaiting renewal, and cut refugees' time to contest losing status to 10 days.
items.detail: Both rules go on public inspection Tuesday and take effect when published in the Federal Register on Oct. 14. The work-permit rule finalizes, without change, an October 2025 interim rule that ended automatic extensions of employment authorization documents (EADs) for people who file renewals on time in certain categories; renewals must now be approved before the old card lapses. The second, an interim rule, cuts the response period after a notice of intent to terminate refugee status from 30 days to 10, with comments due in 30 days. DHS and the Justice Department also finalized their June 2025 rule speeding civil fines for migrants who fail to leave or who cross illegally, the policy a Boston judge blocked Oct. 6.
items.why: Workers caught in USCIS renewal backlogs can lose the right to work, and refugees get far less time to fight termination.

items.text: Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv overnight with no warning from partners, Zelenskyy said, as a strike on a Kharkiv apartment building killed four.
items.detail: Zelenskyy said Russia attacked overnight with more than 100 drones, loitering munitions and ballistic missiles; five ballistic missiles struck civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, where one person was killed and 11 injured, the UN said. In Kharkiv a residential building was destroyed, four people were killed and 41 injured in one evening. Zelenskyy said Ukraine got no intelligence from partners about the missiles headed to Kyiv; Ukrainian officials said U.S. intelligence sharing continues. He said Ukraine has not struck Russian refineries since President Trump announced an energy ceasefire, while Russia keeps hitting Ukraine's energy sites. On Monday U.S. officials warned they could suspend intelligence sharing.
items.why: Early missile warnings save lives, and Washington has threatened to cut off the intelligence that provides them.

items.text: JPMorgan Chase missed quarterly profit estimates for the first time in nearly three years, while Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo beat them.
items.detail: JPMorgan earned $15.3 billion, or $5.57 a share, up from $5.07 a year earlier but below the $5.85 analysts expected (LSEG); it was its first miss since late 2023. Goldman earned $5.29 billion, or $17.01 a share, versus $13.02 expected, on equities trading. Citi reported $2.85 a share on $23.85 billion revenue; Wells Fargo earned $1.87 a share but missed on revenue at $21.87 billion. Executives said dealmaking and bond trading slowed in late September as the Iran war, inflation and rising yields rattled markets. Bank of America and Morgan Stanley report Wednesday.
items.why: Big-bank results are the first broad read on how higher rates and war-driven volatility are hitting the economy.

items.text: UnitedHealth Group raised its full-year profit outlook after beating estimates, and Johnson & Johnson also raised guidance despite a talc-litigation charge.
items.detail: UnitedHealth earned $4.69 a share adjusted ($4.56 reported) on $112.7 billion revenue, versus $4.14 expected (LSEG), and now expects 2026 adjusted earnings of at least $20.50 a share, up from $19.50 to $20. Its medical cost ratio was 88.4%. J&J's sales rose 5.9% to $25.4 billion, but earnings fell to 9 cents a share from $2.12 on a one-time charge for its proposed ovarian talc litigation resolution and two deals; adjusted earnings were $2.59. J&J raised its 2026 sales outlook to about $101.2 billion and adjusted earnings to $11.10 a share.
items.why: The largest U.S. private insurer and the largest U.S. health-products maker both said business is stronger than they expected.

items.text: Sales of previously owned U.S. homes rose 1.5% in September to a 3.99 million annual pace but stayed below a year earlier, the Realtors said.
items.detail: The National Association of Realtors said sales fell 2.2% from September 2025; August was revised down to 3.93 million, and the two months were the year's slowest. Inventory rose to 1.60 million homes, the most since November 2019, or 4.8 months of supply. The median price rose 1.3% from a year earlier to $417,500, and homes sat a median 33 days. Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed rate averaged 6.86% in September and was 7.40% as of Oct. 8. October sales come out Nov. 12.
items.why: Higher mortgage rates are keeping the housing market near its slowest pace in years.

items.text: BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, upgraded U.S. Treasuries for the first time in about six years and cut U.S. stocks to neutral.
items.detail: In its weekly commentary the BlackRock Investment Institute moved short-term Treasuries to overweight and long-term Treasuries to neutral, ending a government-bond underweight it had held for most of the period since October 2020, when the 10-year yield was 0.9%. The 10-year yield is about 5.25%, near 2002 levels, up about 110 basis points this year. BlackRock said market expectations of about 160 basis points more Fed tightening over the next year look overdone, and called the U.S. stock downgrade a short-term risk-management move; it still prefers AI and tech within stocks.
items.why: A firm managing more than $15 trillion is betting the bond selloff that has pushed up borrowing costs has gone far enough.

items.text: Martin Shkreli should be held in contempt for trading drug-company stocks despite a lifetime pharma ban, the FTC and seven states told a federal judge.
items.detail: In filings Tuesday in Manhattan federal court, the FTC and the attorneys general of New York, California, Illinois, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Virginia said Shkreli violated Judge Denise Cote's 2022 injunction by trading stocks of at least 60 pharmaceutical companies and discussing and advising on their businesses on livestreams and social media. They asked the court to force him to sell his pharma holdings, give up his trading profits and face more fines or jail for future violations, and to bar him, his sister and his partner from destroying evidence. The 2022 ban followed his raising the price of the HIV drug Daraprim from $17.50 to $750 a pill. Shkreli's representatives did not immediately comment.
items.why: Regulators are trying to enforce one of the few lifetime industry bans a court has imposed.

items.text: The Trump administration may not cut any more trees at Washington's East Potomac Golf Links through Oct. 26, a federal judge ordered.
items.detail: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes also required three business days' notice before any irreversible change to the public course, which President Trump plans to overhaul. The National Park Service felled about 430 trees there Saturday, a Justice Department lawyer said, after notifying the court just before 5 p.m. Friday; about 99 more were marked for removal. At a nearly four-hour hearing Monday, Reyes told government lawyers they had "lost credibility" and ordered Park Service officials to testify about who approved the cutting. The D.C. Preservation League and two golfers brought the suit. A hearing is set for Oct. 19.
items.why: A court has stepped in after hundreds of mature trees on a historic public course came down in one day.

items.text: Ledger said hidden cellular chips inside some of its crypto wallets, sold by reseller CryptoBilis, stole users' recovery phrases.
items.detail: In an investigation update Tuesday, Ledger said the implant sat inside the device case, read the 24-word recovery phrase off the screen during setup and sent it over a mobile network using an eSIM. It said the chip did not alter the secure chip, operating system or transactions, calling it a physical supply-chain attack rather than a breach of its software. Every confirmed loss from the Oct. 9 thefts involved a device sold by CryptoBilis, which has stopped selling Ledger signers. Electronics chain MediaMarkt Saturn also halted Ledger sales after a customer in Germany found an implant. Ledger has not confirmed the number of victims; on-chain researchers estimated losses up to $93 million across more than 300 wallets.
items.why: It is a rare confirmed hardware tampering attack on a widely used crypto wallet brand.

items.text: Cornell suspended all parties and social events at its fraternity houses for the rest of the 2026-27 academic year, citing the Jane Doe case.
items.detail: In a letter Tuesday, President Michael Kotlikoff said the suspension covers all Interfraternity Council houses, takes effect immediately and allows a review of whether and how fraternity life can safely continue; any fraternity that holds an in-house party or social event will face an immediate emergency suspension. He apologized for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024. Cornell will also add staff to its Office of Civil Rights and victim-advocate office, and is working with the New York State Police so its investigators, who are independent of the university, can investigate on-campus sexual assault reports while Sally Yates's independent review runs. Attorney General Letitia James's separate criminal investigation continues; no one has been criminally charged, and the men named in the civil lawsuit deny the accusations.
items.why: Cornell is acting on campus safety now rather than waiting for its outside review or the state's criminal inquiry.

items.text: A federal rule barring Medicaid and CHIP money for puberty blockers, hormones and gender surgery for minors takes effect today in every state.
items.detail: The CMS final rule, published Aug. 13 (91 FR 52406), bars federal Medicaid funding for these procedures for patients under 18 and federal CHIP funding for those under 19. Children already on hormone therapy get up to six months of federal funding to taper; that transition does not cover puberty blockers or surgery. In New Hampshire, families suing in Goe v. HHS were denied a temporary restraining order on Oct. 5; their preliminary-injunction request is still pending, and no court has blocked the rule.
items.why: It ends federal payment for this care for low-income children nationwide, shifting the cost to states or families.

items.text: A second drone attack in a week off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast sank one ship and damaged a Ukrainian-owned vessel, Bulgaria's prime minister said.
items.detail: Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the Maltese-flagged, Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3 was hit by three drones about 18 nautical miles off Bulgaria at about 1:30 a.m. Tuesday local time (6:30 p.m. ET Monday); its 15 crew were rescued and five got medical help. One crew member from the ship that sank was also rescued. Radev said there was no clear evidence who attacked but that "the outcome benefits" Russia, said Russia's ambassador would be summoned, and planned to speak with NATO chief Mark Rutte. Last week drones hit two ships off Bulgaria, sinking one whose 10 crew are still missing.
items.why: Repeated drone strikes next to a NATO member's waters raise the risk of the war spilling into the alliance.

items.text: New drones and other devices built with chips or circuit boards from FCC blacklisted firms such as DJI can no longer win FCC approval, starting today.
items.detail: The FCC's Third Report and Order (FCC 26-50, ET Docket 21-232), published in the Federal Register Sept. 11, closes the "component part loophole" by barring authorization of devices that contain logic-bearing hardware made by Covered List entities, even if assembled in the U.S. It applies to applications filed on or after Oct. 13; already authorized equipment is unaffected, and pending applications are exempt unless amended to change such parts. It also requires online marketplaces to show the FCC ID at the point of sale.
items.why: It shuts a workaround U.S. assemblers used to keep selling new products built around Chinese drone and router parts.

items.text: Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, a voter on rates this year, said the Fed needs a restrictive policy stance to bring inflation back to 2%.
items.detail: In remarks to the NABE annual meeting in Cleveland, Hammack said "a restrictive monetary policy stance is appropriate to ensure a timely return to 2 percent inflation" and that she prefers smaller adjustments made "relatively quickly." She cited August headline PCE inflation of 3.4% and core of 3%, called price pressures broad-based (tariffs, energy and the AI buildout), and noted unemployment steady at 4.2%. She said a clear weakening in the job market would change her view.
items.why: A voting Fed official openly leaning toward tighter policy signals borrowing costs may not fall soon.

items.text: U.S. pending home sales fell 4% in September, the biggest monthly drop in over three years, as mortgage rates topped 7%, Redfin said.
items.detail: Redfin said pending sales hit their lowest level since spring 2014 outside April 2020, and fell from a year earlier in all 50 of the most populous metros, led by Seattle (-24.4%). 14.5% of September contracts were canceled, the highest share on record outside March–April 2020. Homes for sale rose to the most since March 2020, and the median sale price rose just 1.3% from a year earlier to $393,895. The weekly average mortgage rate hit 7.28% at the end of September. NAR's official existing-home sales report is due at 10 a.m. ET today.
items.why: Higher mortgage rates are freezing home buying and starting to cool prices.

items.text: The EU sanctioned nearly 1,600 Russian companies and executives in its largest listings package aimed at Moscow's military industry.
items.detail: The Council adopted 1,569 listings — 826 companies and 743 CEOs — targeting mid-level suppliers of electronics, missiles, drones and aircraft parts; more than half address ballistic-missile production. Listed people face asset freezes and EU travel bans, and the Ukraine territorial-integrity sanctions list now totals nearly 4,600. Separately the same day, the Council listed 77 people over illegal Russian State Duma elections in occupied Ukrainian territory.
items.why: The biggest EU listing round since 2022 raises pressure on Russia's war industry as Washington eases energy sanctions on Moscow.

items.text: U.S. officials warned Ukraine and European allies they could suspend intelligence sharing and PURL weapons buys if Kyiv keeps striking Russian energy sites.
items.detail: CNN reported Monday that State Department and Pentagon warnings went out over the weekend, confirming an earlier Financial Times account; a NATO official said PURL supplies were still flowing Monday. PURL is the Europe-funded channel for buying U.S. weapons for Ukraine, including scarce Patriot interceptors. The White House declined comment. The pressure followed President Trump's announced energy ceasefire and his criticism of President Zelensky.
items.why: Cutting intelligence and Patriot supply would immediately weaken Ukraine's air defense.

items.text: Evernorth Holdings began Nasdaq trading as XRPN, the first pure-play publicly listed XRP treasury company.
items.detail: Yahoo Finance marked XRPN newly listed effective Oct. 12; shares opened at $16.68, ranged from $16.39 to $19.39, and closed at $16.91 on about 1.28 million shares. Evernorth closed its Armada Acquisition Corp. II merger on Oct. 9 and says it holds about 473 million XRP with roughly $300 million in gross cash proceeds. Warrants trade as XRPNW.
items.why: Turns a closely watched crypto SPAC into a traded XRP-treasury stock on a federal holiday.

items.text: A second man accused in the Cornell assault case asked a Tompkins County criminal court to bar Attorney General Letitia James from leading any grand jury in the case.
items.detail: Lawyers for Winston Lee, one of seven men named in Jane Doe's civil lawsuit, filed the motion Oct. 9, arguing that James's Sept. 28 social media post supporting Jane Doe shows she prejudged the case. They asked the court to keep James from running the criminal investigation, to poll any future grand jurors on whether they saw her comments, and to schedule arguments. James's office said it is committed to reviewing only the facts, the evidence and the law. This motion is separate from Gillio Lopes's petition in Albany County, which is set for oral arguments on Oct. 29. James remains special prosecutor, no one has been criminally charged, and Lee and Lopes deny the accusations.
items.why: Two defendants are now asking two different courts to remove the state's lead prosecutor before any grand jury hears the case.

items.text: The WHO issued a formal outbreak notice on the Irkutsk lab worker's death, finding no evidence of ongoing transmission but no confirmed cause.
items.detail: In a Disease Outbreak News report, the WHO said Russia confirmed the 28-year-old Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute employee died Oct. 2 of severe pneumonia, that she and all contacts tested negative for high-threat pathogens, and that contacts stayed symptom-free. The WHO said it has found no evidence of ongoing transmission, but the lack of a confirmed diagnosis remains a key uncertainty.
items.why: The WHO's official assessment lowers outbreak fears while leaving the cause of death unresolved.

items.text: Riyadh's airport attack Saturday killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, Saudi authorities said, and the Houthis claimed the strike.
items.detail: It was the third Houthi attack this week on King Khalid International Airport; the earlier two killed four people. The missile hit without warning, all flights were diverted and operations were temporarily suspended, and FlightAware counted at least 291 cancellations in 24 hours. The U.S. Embassy told Americans to avoid the airport. President Trump said the U.S. was weighing whether to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis.
items.why: The deadliest strike yet on a Gulf civilian airport in the Iran war's Yemen front.

items.text: President Trump said Ukraine should replace Volodymyr Zelensky, a day after Zelensky called Trump's Russian diesel deal a sign of weakness.
items.detail: "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," Trump told reporters Saturday, blaming Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for high diesel prices. Ukraine has been under martial law since 2022, which suspends elections. Russia's government said Saturday it partially lifted its diesel export ban with immediate effect to fill the deal.
items.why: The sharpest U.S. break with Kyiv since the war began, as Washington buys Russian fuel.

items.text: An Erie, Pennsylvania, man killed eight people, including relatives, a pregnant woman and two young children, at his home Friday before killing himself, police said.
items.detail: Police Chief Rick Lorah said the 45-year-old was related to seven of the victims; two women shot outside had arrived and pounded on the door. Gov. Josh Shapiro offered state support. Separately, Philadelphia police officer Shane Seiber, 40, was killed and a colleague critically wounded in a shotgun ambush early Saturday; a city water department employee was arrested.
items.why: One of Pennsylvania's deadliest shootings in years, on the same weekend a Philadelphia officer was killed.

items.text: Isaias's remnants spun up tornadoes in Georgia and South Carolina Saturday, destroying or damaging at least four buildings in Burke County, Ga.
items.detail: The National Weather Service confirmed a tornado near Appleton in Allendale County, S.C., that moved into Barnwell County, and damage in Screven County, Ga. No injuries were reported in Burke County. Forecasters warned of flooding as the storm's remnants move toward the Tennessee Valley and Mid-Atlantic.
items.why: Isaias's damage is spreading well inland from the Gulf Coast.

items.text: A federal judge struck down the Justice Department's nationwide program for collecting states' unredacted voter rolls, vacating it for the whole country.
items.detail: In a 78-page opinion dated Friday, Oct. 9, U.S. District Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia set aside DOJ's "Voter List Maintenance Policy" in Common Cause v. U.S. Department of Justice, brought by Common Cause and four voters against DOJ and the attorney general. Under the policy, begun in May 2025, the Civil Rights Division requested full voter lists, including names, birth dates, addresses and driver's license or partial Social Security numbers, from 49 states and the District of Columbia, shared the data with Homeland Security to run through the SAVE citizenship database, and urged states to remove voters it deemed ineligible. The court said at least 18 states fully cooperated; others refused, and at least 25 federal district courts have dismissed DOJ suits to force them. The judge ruled that no statute, including the 1960 Civil Rights Act, the National Voter Registration Act or the Help America Vote Act, authorizes DOJ to collect and share unredacted statewide rolls; that DOJ ignored the risk of removing citizens based on records known to be unreliable; and that the policy violated the Privacy Act and the Paperwork Reduction Act. She rejected DOJ's request to limit relief to the plaintiffs, citing the APA's ordinary remedy of vacatur. The ruling does not stop states from maintaining their own rolls.
items.why: It halts the federal government's nationwide voter-data and citizenship-check program less than four weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms, including in states that already handed over their rolls.
items.court: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia
items.source: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (opinion)

items.text: Ukrainian drones attacked Russia's Rostov region overnight, injuring six and starting a fire in Rostov-on-Don, hours after the U.S. eased sanctions on Russian diesel.
items.detail: Rostov Gov. Yury Slyusar said more than 100 drones were downed over the region. Six people were hurt; apartment buildings and houses in Rostov-on-Don and an unoccupied building in Bataysk were damaged, two vessels were hit at the port of Azov, a railway bridge was damaged and later reopened, and firefighters were putting out a blaze at what he called warehouse industrial facilities. Russia's Defense Ministry said it downed 560 Ukrainian drones over 17 regions. Geolocated video and NASA satellite fire data placed the Rostov-on-Don blaze at an oil-products export terminal linked to the Novoshakhtinsk refinery; neither Moscow nor Kyiv has confirmed the terminal was hit, and no official has said its fuel was bound for the United States. The attack came hours after Treasury licensed Russian diesel sales, including imports into the U.S., through April 7, 2027.
items.why: Kyiv's strikes on Russian fuel infrastructure are colliding with Washington's new deal to bring Russian diesel to market.

items.text: One of the men accused in the Cornell assault case asked a New York court to remove Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor.
items.detail: Gillio Lopes, one of seven men named in Jane Doe's civil lawsuit, filed an Article 78 petition in Albany County Supreme Court on Oct. 7 arguing that Gov. Kathy Hochul's appointment of James is improper. The filing points to James's Sept. 28 social media post supporting Jane Doe, three days before her appointment, as evidence of bias, and asks the court to void the appointment and name a different prosecutor. A judge's order schedules oral arguments for Oct. 29. James remains special prosecutor, no criminal charges have been filed, and the men deny wrongdoing.
items.why: A court will now weigh whether the state's lead prosecutor can stay on the reopened criminal investigation.

items.text: The UAE attorney general said the Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash FZ1073 into Ben Gurion Airport's passenger terminal in a suicide attack.
items.detail: In a statement carried Friday by the UAE state news agency WAM, Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said investigators found the 29-year-old Omani co-pilot had developed a premeditated plot to seize the aircraft and strike the terminal to cause the greatest possible loss of life, and had used two earlier Tel Aviv trips to study the route and airport. He said the suspect confessed in the presence of his lawyer and claimed he acted alone, while investigators keep checking for accomplices or other links. A pilot assigned to the return flight entered the cockpit, restrained the co-pilot with a cabin crew member and passengers, and the crew landed in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Flydubai said it is supporting the investigation. No charges have been announced.
items.why: This is the UAE's first official account of the intended target and the plot behind the Sept. 30 attack.

items.text: Microsoft, Adobe and six major IT outsourcing firms were suspended from the Labor Department program employers use to sponsor foreign workers for green cards.
items.detail: Vice President JD Vance announced the move Thursday at a White House Fraud Task Force news conference, citing alleged fraud, and said that for every worker Microsoft laid off it hired "one and a half foreign indentured servants." Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the department is suspending Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini from the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program, the required step before an employer can sponsor a worker, including H-1B visa holders, for a green card, and is suspending Microsoft and Adobe because of multiple active federal investigations. Officials gave no end date. Sonderling also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, will be investigated over allegedly bringing in international students to undercut American wages; Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had been served. Microsoft did not immediately comment.
items.why: Freezes a key step toward green cards for foreign workers at eight large tech employers as the administration targets alleged abuse of work-visa programs.

items.text: Russia's health watchdog called reports of a second person infected by the dead Irkutsk plague-lab worker fake; the WHO says it still doesn't know what killed her.
items.detail: In a statement Thursday, Rospotrebnadzor rejected reports that a second person fell ill after contact with the 28-year-old Anti-Plague Institute lab worker, AP reported; it gave no new information on her illness or death. On Wednesday the agency said there was no risk of an epidemic, that nearly 5,000 lab tests found no dangerous pathogens, that 90% of those quarantined had been released and that it was winding down its precautionary measures, Reuters reported. It also said she had been vaccinated and had immunity to dangerous infections, and that a biosafety check at the institute found no emergencies in handling pathogens. Maria Van Kerkhove, the WHO's epidemic and pandemic chief, said Wednesday the agency does not know the causative agent of the Oct. 2 death and cannot make a fuller risk assessment without more information from Russia. Russia still calls it pneumonia of unknown cause and says no plague case has been registered in the Irkutsk region.
items.why: Russia is winding down its emergency measures and denying any spread while the WHO says it still lacks the cause of death.

items.text: Isaias became the Atlantic season's first hurricane, and hurricane warnings now cover the coast from Mississippi to the Florida Panhandle.
items.detail: At 5 a.m. ET Thursday, NOAA Hurricane Hunters put Isaias's top sustained winds at 80 mph, about 420 miles south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River, moving east-northeast at 9 mph. A hurricane warning covers Ocean Springs, Miss., to the Bay/Gulf County line in Florida, and a storm surge warning runs from the mouth of the Mississippi to the Steinhatchee River, with 5 to 7 feet of surge possible from Ocean Springs to Indian Pass and in Mobile Bay. The National Hurricane Center expects 3 to 7 inches of rain, up to 10 in spots, from southeast Louisiana to the Panhandle, and says Isaias should be a strong hurricane by landfall late Friday or early Saturday.
items.why: Coastal Mississippi, Alabama and the Florida Panhandle have about a day and a half to finish preparing, and flooding rain could reach inland.

items.text: Oil prices jumped about 4%, with Brent crude near $104 a barrel, on Gulf tanker attacks and Gulf of Mexico shutdowns ahead of Hurricane Isaias.
items.detail: Brent, the international benchmark, rose 3.8% to about $104 a barrel in early Thursday trading. Tanker attacks tied to the Iran war are at their highest of the conflict, and Shell and Chevron said they were shutting in Gulf of Mexico production as Isaias approaches. The 10-year Treasury yield rose 5 basis points to 5.331%, and Japan's Nikkei fell 1.4%. Prices were from early trading and can move during the day.
items.why: Higher oil and bond yields feed into fuel, shipping and borrowing costs.

items.text: Houthi attacks on airports in Riyadh and Abha killed three people and wounded 36, Saudi Arabia said; the Saudi-led coalition then struck 82 Houthi targets.
items.detail: Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said Abha International Airport and Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport were attacked on Oct. 6 and 7; an Egyptian and an Algerian were killed at Abha and a Sudanese national in Riyadh. The Houthis said they fired a ballistic missile at the Riyadh airport, their second claimed attack on it this week; the coalition said that missile was intercepted. The coalition said it then destroyed 82 military targets, including mountain missile sites and command centers, AFP reported.
items.why: The Yemen fighting is now killing people at the Saudi capital's main airport and drawing large Saudi airstrikes.

items.text: The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration over $20 million in taxpayer-funded TV ads it calls illegal pro-Trump propaganda.
items.detail: The complaint, filed Wednesday in U.S. District Court in Washington, names President Trump, the White House, Homeland Security and the Office of Management and Budget, and asks the court to declare the ads illegal and stop federal money from paying for them. The ads, marked 'Paid for by the U.S. Government,' began airing in September; $20 million has been drawn from a $175 million DHS immigration-enforcement fund, and more than $12 million had been spent so far, AP reported, citing AdImpact. No ruling yet.
items.why: A court test of whether federal money can pay for ads praising the president weeks before the midterms.

items.text: Texas executed Jamaal Howard, the first U.S. execution since Tennessee's failed lethal injection of Christa Pike a week earlier.
items.detail: Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8:03 p.m. CT Wednesday in Huntsville after a dose of pentobarbital, the same drug used on Pike. He was convicted of killing store clerk Vickie Swartout in a 2000 robbery. The Supreme Court denied his requests to stop the execution; only Justice Jackson said she would grant a stay. AP said it was the 30th U.S. execution this year.
items.why: Executions are going ahead with pentobarbital despite the Pike failure.

items.text: The tanker Acers was hit by multiple projectiles about 50 nautical miles north of Qatar, with casualties, Britain's UKMTO said.
items.detail: UKMTO said the master reported the strike at about 3 p.m. ET Wednesday, about 50 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, Qatar; it gave no casualty count. Maritime security firm Vanguard Tech identified the ship as the Antigua-flagged, Greek-managed tanker Acers. It is the first reported tanker attack in the western Gulf in weeks, far from the Strait of Hormuz.
items.why: Tanker attacks are spreading beyond Hormuz into Gulf waters off Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.

items.text: Wells Fargo's programs to raise Black homeownership are under a Fair Housing Act investigation by HUD.
items.detail: HUD Secretary Scott Turner announced the probe Oct. 7, and HUD sent a letter to Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf saying it will examine whether the bank offered different products or terms based on race. The programs date to the bank's 2017 pledge of $60 billion in loans to add 250,000 Black homeowners by 2027, expanded in 2022 to refinancing for minority homeowners. Findings could lead to charges or a Justice Department referral; this is an investigation, not a finding.
items.why: A federal civil-rights probe of one of the largest U.S. mortgage lenders over race-focused lending.
items.source: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development

items.text: Pennsylvania's measles outbreak reached 1,078 cases in 41 counties this year, with 207 hospitalizations and five deaths, the state health department said.
items.detail: The Oct. 7 update added 74 cases since Oct. 5; the department said more than 40 of them were people who got sick more than two weeks earlier and were reported late. Four cases were in vaccinated people. Statewide MMR doses rose from about 25,000 in a typical month to more than 56,000 in September.
items.why: One of the largest U.S. measles outbreaks in years, with five deaths.

items.text: The CFTC asked for public comment on federal rules for leveraged retail crypto trades and a new exchange category for crypto, called a crypto asset market.
items.detail: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission's advance notice of proposed rulemaking covers 'Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions' and 'Regulation Crypto Asset Markets,' including whether to make crypto asset markets a subcategory of designated contract markets. Comments are due 60 days after the notice appears in the Federal Register. Chairman Michael S. Selig said the rules aim to prevent schemes like FTX.
items.why: The first formal step toward CFTC rules for U.S. crypto exchanges and leveraged retail crypto trading.

items.text: Tropical Storm Isaias put the northern Gulf Coast under a hurricane watch, with forecasters warning it could hit as a major hurricane late Friday.
items.detail: The National Hurricane Center's hurricane watch runs from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, to Indian Pass on the Florida Panhandle, with a storm surge watch from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Yankeetown, Fla., and tropical storm watches on either side. As of 1 p.m. CDT, Hurricane Hunters found Isaias strengthening, with 50 mph winds about 520 miles south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi, moving east-northeast at 8 mph. NHC director Michael Brennan said it could reach Category 3 before landfall late Friday or early Saturday. Florida declared a state of emergency for more than a third of its counties, and producers shut in a significant share of Gulf offshore oil and gas output, AP reported.
items.why: Coastal residents from Louisiana to Florida's Big Bend now have formal watches, with energy output and weekend travel already affected.

items.text: Russia's overnight attack on Ukraine killed at least 30 people, up from 11 this morning, including 19 in a Pryluky apartment building.
items.detail: A Russian cruise missile hit a residential building in Pryluky, Chernihiv region, killing 19 people, five of them children, and injuring 55, Ukraine's emergency service said as rescuers kept searching the rubble. Authorities count at least 30 dead and 138 injured across Ukraine over the past day, including three in Kyiv and two each in Kremenchuk, Kirovohrad and Sumy regions. Ukraine's Air Force said Russia fired ballistic missiles, 48 cruise missiles (39 stopped) and 130 drones (117 stopped).
items.why: The toll nearly tripled during the day, making it the deadliest Russian strike on Ukraine in about a month.

items.text: Fed minutes show most officials expected another interest-rate increase by year-end, according to the September meeting record released Wednesday.
items.detail: At the Sept. 15–16 meeting the FOMC voted 12–0 to raise its target range a quarter point to 3.75%–4%. The minutes say most participants judged another increase would likely be appropriate by year-end and saw inflation risks skewed to the upside, citing energy prices and AI-driven investment. Staff estimated August PCE inflation at 3.8% (core 3.4%) and no longer see inflation returning to 2% until 2029. The next meeting is Oct. 27–28. Earlier Wednesday, Treasury sold $39 billion of 10-year notes at 5.300% with a 2.77 bid-to-cover, stronger than average demand two days after the 10-year yield hit a 2002 high.
items.why: A second hike this year would push borrowing and mortgage costs higher still.

items.text: Tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz reached at least 12 last week, the most of any week since the U.S.-Iran war began, Reuters reported.
items.detail: Three maritime security sources counted at least 12 attacks on oil, LNG and LPG tankers around the strait from Sept. 28 to Oct. 5, the highest weekly count since the war began Feb. 28; the UN's International Maritime Organization recorded nine incidents that week. Separately, an adviser to Iran's Revolutionary Guards, Brig. Gen. Mohammadreza Naqdi, said Wednesday that routes along Oman's coast would soon be blocked and that the strait stays closed until Iran's demands are met.
items.why: Rising attacks threaten the oil and gas exports Gulf producers are still pushing through the strait.

items.text: Optional Practical Training for foreign students would cost $70,000 per student under a Homeland Security proposal filed Wednesday.
items.detail: The ICE proposed rule, filed for public inspection Oct. 7 and set to publish Oct. 8, would charge $70,000 for an F-1 student's first OPT period and $30,000 for each later one; schools would recommend OPT only for students whose fee they pay. DHS says that without the fees it may shut the program down entirely. Comments are due 30 days after publication. It is a proposal, not a final rule.
items.why: OPT is the main way foreign graduates of U.S. colleges start working here and feeds the H-1B pipeline.

items.text: An 18-year-old was charged with planning a terror attack on the Mall of America after buying an AK-47 from undercover FBI agents, prosecutors say.
items.detail: Federal prosecutors in Minnesota say Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, a U.S.-born citizen, was arrested Tuesday in a Richfield park after paying $600 for an AK-47 and 200 rounds to an undercover FBI employee posing as an ISIS member. The complaint alleges he told an informant he planned to kill non-Muslims at the mall on Oct. 24. U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said he spoke of killing 30 to 60 people. He made his first court appearance Wednesday in St. Paul; the charges are allegations.
items.why: A foiled plot against the country's best-known mall, announced by federal prosecutors.

items.text: Britain's Court of Appeal threw out the fraud convictions of five former Barclays traders jailed in the Libor and Euribor rate-rigging scandal.
items.detail: The court cleared Jay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon and Colin Bermingham, each convicted of conspiracy to defraud; four served prison time. The Serious Fraud Office did not oppose the appeals, which followed the UK Supreme Court's July 2025 ruling clearing Tom Hayes and Carlo Palombo. Only two UK rate-rigging convictions now stand, and one of them, Christian Bittar's, is set for appeal Oct. 9.
items.why: Most of Britain's criminal cases from the benchmark-rigging scandal that touched mortgage and loan rates have now collapsed.

items.text: Social Security identity-theft victims will get a single point of contact at the agency under a law President Trump signed Wednesday.
items.detail: H.R. 5345, the Improving Social Security's Service to Victims of Identity Theft Act, requires the Social Security Administration to give one point of contact to people whose number has been misused or whose card was lost. Trump also signed S. 766, the Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act, which requires a yearly report on federally funded projects more than five years behind schedule or more than $1 billion over budget.
items.why: It changes how the agency handles victims of Social Security number theft.

items.text: Imports worth $2,500 or less would face tighter filing and bond rules under a Customs and Border Protection proposal filed Wednesday.
items.detail: The CBP proposed rule, filed for public inspection Oct. 7 and set to publish Oct. 8, would change filing rules for informal entries of $2,500 or less, create a new electronic entry type for mailed packages, require mail carriers to send an extra data element, and require a basic import bond for some informal entries. Comments are due 60 days after publication.
items.why: It covers the flood of small online orders, so added rules could raise costs or slow cheap imports.

items.text: Saudi Arabia launched an air-safety investigation into the Flydubai FZ1073 cockpit attack, separate from the UAE's criminal probe, Reuters reported.
items.detail: Three people close to the matter told Reuters on Wednesday that Saudi Arabia notified aviation agencies abroad it will run a safety investigation under international rules, because the flight was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked the captain with an axe. The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board confirmed it assigned a representative, since the Boeing 737 MAX was built in the United States. Saudi authorities did not comment, and it is unclear whether findings will be published. Israel's Aircraft Safety Investigation Authority said Israel offered to take part but has not been invited. The UAE-led criminal investigation, which its prosecutor general calls a terrorist attack, continues; no charges have been announced.
items.why: A second, technical investigation now runs alongside the UAE criminal case, with U.S. safety investigators involved.

items.text: New York Attorney General Letitia James's office said the Tompkins County DA agreed to cooperate with its Cornell criminal investigation.
items.detail: A spokesperson for James said Tuesday that the investigation is led by the office's Criminal Justice Division and began Thursday evening after the governor's appointment. Since then the office has spoken with District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, Jane Doe's attorney, and several candidates for outside counsel to support the investigation. Van Houten has said his office will cooperate fully. No criminal charges have been filed, and the seven men named in the civil lawsuit deny wrongdoing.
items.why: The state's criminal inquiry is staffing up with the local prosecutor's cooperation, separate from Cornell's own review.

items.text: WHO chief Tedros asked Russia what killed the Irkutsk plague-lab worker and whether a second employee has pneumonia; the Kremlin says it informed the WHO properly.
items.detail: Tedros said Wednesday on X that the WHO has asked Russia to clarify the cause of the 28-year-old lab technician's severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the quarantine and other public-health measures, and media reports of a second institute employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause, adding that timely, complete and transparent sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential, Reuters reported. Russia has not confirmed a second case, and Reuters said it found no evidence of reports that a second person in Siberia had died. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that Russia notified the WHO in line with established procedures, called much of the coverage false and told people to rely on Rospotrebnadzor; he was responding to an ABC News report that the U.S. lodged a formal diplomatic complaint over Moscow's handling of the case. Peskov said no Putin–Trump call is scheduled yet, after Trump said Tuesday he would speak to Putin "very soon" about it. Russia still calls the Oct. 2 death pneumonia of unknown cause and has not said what caused it.
items.why: The WHO is now publicly pressing Moscow for the cause of death and a possible second case, while Russia insists it has disclosed enough.

items.text: A federal judge in Boston blocked the Trump administration's policy of fining migrants up to $1.8 million for not leaving the U.S. after final deportation orders.
items.detail: U.S. District Judge George O'Toole stayed the ICE rule used to impose the fines and barred enforcement of fines issued after June 27, 2025, while a class-action lawsuit brought by two fined migrants moves forward, Reuters reported Monday. He found the fines were likely imposed unlawfully, including because ICE skipped public notice and comment and the Department of Homeland Security did not consider individual circumstances. Since last year the administration has levied fines of $998 a day, applied retroactively for up to five years. DHS said in July it had issued more than 100,000 such fines totaling about $84 billion.
items.why: The order halts collection of more than 100,000 fines worth about $84 billion while the case proceeds.

items.text: Evernorth said an administrative delay moved the expected Armada II deal close to about Oct. 9 and XRPN's Nasdaq debut to about Oct. 12.
items.detail: In an Oct. 6 SEC Form 8-K, Evernorth Holdings said the delay is not expected to affect the closing. Closing remains subject to customary conditions, and Nasdaq trading of Class A shares under ticker XRPN depends on those conditions and listing requirements. The prior schedule had called for a close about Oct. 7 and trading about Oct. 8. Armada II shareholders approved the business combination on Sept. 30.
items.why: Pushes back a closely watched XRP-treasury SPAC close and Nasdaq listing by a few days; dates are still estimates.

items.text: Drones sank one merchant ship and set another on fire inside Bulgaria's Black Sea economic zone, Bulgaria said; the sunken ship's crew is missing.
items.detail: Sea and air drones hit the two ships about 70 nautical miles east of Byala early Tuesday local time. The Togo-flagged, Turkish-owned Alfa Watan sank and its crew is unaccounted for. The Palau-flagged Able, carrying wheat, caught fire; all 18 crew were rescued and taken to Varna, and one is in critical condition with severe burns. Prime Minister Rumen Radev called the attack "absolutely unacceptable" and said the drones were "clearly either Russian or Ukrainian"; who launched them has not been established. Bulgaria is in contact with NATO, and President Iliana Iotova called a national security council meeting for Wednesday.
items.why: A ship was sunk inside a NATO member's waters, spreading the war's shipping risk to the western Black Sea and the grain trade.

items.text: The S&P 500 closed at a record high Tuesday, its first since August, as Treasury yields eased from their highest levels since 2002.
items.detail: The S&P 500 rose 44.98 points, or 0.6%, to 7,818.93. The Dow gained 253.38 to 51,521.28, and the Nasdaq rose 122.48 to 27,599.79, its second straight record. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 5.28% from 5.31% late Monday. The S&P 500 is up 23% from its late-March low.
items.why: Stocks hit an all-time high even as the Iran war and high bond yields weigh on the economy.

items.text: Twelve sailors were injured when a projectile hit the tanker On Peace in the Strait of Hormuz, India's foreign ministry said.
items.detail: India said 12 of the Panama-flagged tanker's 19 crew were hurt, 11 of them Indian, and Oman helped evacuate them to Khasab for treatment. India did not say who carried out the attack.
