The ship appears to be the tanker UKMTO reported hit Monday evening with an engine-room fire, though that has not been formally confirmed.
items.why: It is the first report of serious crew injuries in the latest wave of Hormuz tanker attacks.
items.source: gCaptain, citing India's Ministry of External Affairs

items.text: A Nigerian Air Force transport plane crashed in Ondo State, killing all 25 people aboard, the Air Force said.
items.detail: The ATR-42, NAF 931, was on a routine flight from Benin City to Lagos when it went down at Igbokoda on Oct. 5. It carried five crew and 20 passengers. On Tuesday the Air Force confirmed there were no survivors, released the victims' names and ordered an investigation.
items.why: Everyone aboard died in one of Nigeria's deadliest military air crashes in recent years.

items.text: World oil production will fall about 5 million barrels a day this year because of the Iran war, the Energy Information Administration projected.
items.detail: In its Oct. 6 Short-Term Energy Outlook, EIA projected world petroleum production falling from a record 106.3 million barrels a day in 2025 to 101.1 million in 2026, and world demand falling from 104.4 million to 102.4 million. The G7 agreed Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves.
items.why: The government's own forecast shows how much the war is cutting global supply, which feeds fuel prices and inflation.

items.text: The 2018 Section 301 tariffs on Chinese goods will stay in place after U.S. industries asked for them to continue, the U.S. Trade Representative said.
items.detail: USTR's notice, "Continuation of Actions: China's Acts, Policies, and Practices Related to Technology Transfer, Intellectual Property, and Innovation" (FR Doc. 2026-20510), went on Federal Register public inspection Tuesday and publishes Oct. 7. It comes out of the second four-year review of the tariffs, which began in May. A companion notice (2026-20511) makes conforming changes to product exclusions.
items.why: It keeps the original Trump-era China tariffs on a large share of imports from China.

items.text: Treasury's Do Not Pay fraud screening now reaches about 99% of federal programs, up from about 4% a year ago, the department said.
items.detail: Treasury said that in fiscal 2026 it added nine new data sources to Do Not Pay, screened more than 2.3 billion records, and deployed new payment verification that checked more than $3.7 trillion in federal payments. Most remaining programs are expected to finish onboarding early in fiscal 2027. The work follows Executive Order 14249 from March 2025.
items.why: It changes how nearly every federal payment program checks for fraud and improper payments.

items.text: The FDA asked for public input on designing the first federally funded clinical trials of ibogaine, a psychedelic, for opioid addiction and PTSD.
items.detail: The request for information (FDA-2026-N-10429) published in the Federal Register Oct. 6. HHS is funding ibogaine development, and the first trials are expected to study adults with opioid use disorder and adults with PTSD. FDA wants comment on dosing, care settings, safety monitoring, eligibility and stopping rules. Comments close Nov. 20.
items.why: The federal government is directly funding and shaping human trials of a psychedelic drug.

items.text: Cornell's trustees hired former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates to lead an independent review of the 2024 Chi Phi assault case.
items.detail: A new Special Committee of Cornell's Board of Trustees said Tuesday that Yates, a partner at King & Spalding, will review how the university prevents and responds to sexual assault and misconduct, including campus police, hearings and discipline, coordination with prosecutors, and oversight of fraternities and sororities. Her team will also examine Cornell's response to the October 2024 allegations by Jane Doe against Chi Phi members, including whether it followed its own policies. Yates will report to the committee, and the board said it intends to share the findings with the Cornell community. The state attorney general's separate criminal investigation continues; no criminal charges have been filed.
items.why: A former top Justice Department official now leads the outside probe of Cornell's handling of the case, alongside the state's criminal inquiry.

items.text: Russia told the WHO no plague case has been recorded in Irkutsk and that the dead lab worker's contacts tested negative; about 60% have left quarantine.
items.detail: WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier read Russia's official reply at a Geneva briefing Tuesday: "No case of this dangerous disease has been recorded in the city of Irkutsk," and tests of everyone identified as a contact were negative for dangerous pathogens, Reuters reported. Rospotrebnadzor again said testing found no microorganisms linked to the 28-year-old Anti-Plague Institute technician's work, and a Shelekhov district official said about 60% of those quarantined have been released. Russia's reply did not say whether plague was ruled out in the worker herself, whom officials say died Oct. 2 of pneumonia of unknown cause. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Russia should share more information and that Washington is watching "hour by hour"; the WHO still rates the risk to the general public as low.
items.why: Russia's first formal answer to the WHO points away from an outbreak, but it still does not say what killed the lab worker.

items.text: The Flydubai co-pilot told UAE interrogators he planned the attack before the airline hired him, two Israeli officials told Reuters.
items.detail: Reuters reported Monday that the Omani co-pilot of flight FZ1073 said he applied to Flydubai after searching for airlines that fly to Tel Aviv, according to two Israeli officials with knowledge of the UAE-led probe. A third source briefed on the investigation said he had planned to crash last Wednesday's flight into Ben-Gurion airport, and had intended to hijack an earlier Tel Aviv flight he operated this year but did not. The UAE has not announced formal charges or publicly named him. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said pilots from countries without diplomatic ties to Israel, including Oman, may not fly there, and he ordered a security review of foreign airlines serving Israel.
items.why: Investigators' accounts now point to a plot planned in advance, and to questions about how the co-pilot was assigned an Israel route at all.

items.text: The Brewers beat the Padres 4-3 on a ninth-inning walk-off and lead their National League Division Series 2-0.
items.detail: Jackson Chourio's two-run single with two outs in the ninth off Mason Miller gave Milwaukee the win Sunday at American Family Field, the Associated Press reported. The Brewers also won Game 1 3-2 on Saturday. Game 3 is Tuesday in San Diego.
items.why: A best-of-five series is one win from the League Championship Series.

items.text: The Braves beat the Dodgers 3-2 in Game 2 to tie their National League Division Series at 1-1.
items.detail: Atlanta won Sunday night at Dodger Stadium after losing Game 1 5-3 on Saturday, CBS Sports and MLB.com reported. Michael Harris II drove in two runs; Max Muncy homered in the ninth for Los Angeles. Game 3 is Tuesday in Atlanta.
items.why: The reigning champions no longer control the series; the next two games are in Atlanta.

items.text: The White Sox and Rays each took Game 1 of their American League Division Series on Saturday.
items.detail: Chicago beat Cleveland 3-0 behind Munetaka Murakami's two-run homer and a combined three-hitter, the Associated Press reported. Tampa Bay beat the Yankees 1-0 on Jonathan Aranda's homer and a one-hitter started by Drew Rasmussen. Game 2s are Monday in Cleveland and St. Petersburg.
items.why: Both AL best-of-five openers are decided; the round continues Monday.

items.text: Brazil's first-round count has Flavio Bolsonaro leading President Lula, short of a majority, with a runoff on Oct. 25.
items.detail: With 100 percent of polling sections counted early Monday, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party had 56,104,503 votes, 47.03 percent of valid votes, and President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party had 53,879,538, 45.16 percent, O Globo reported from Superior Electoral Court data. Augusto Cury was third with 2.89 percent. Neither reached the more than 50 percent of valid votes needed to win outright, so the two meet in a runoff on Oct. 25. Abstention was about 21 percent, the highest since 1998.
items.why: The presidency of Latin America's largest economy is undecided, and the next vote is set for Oct. 25.

items.text: Rospotrebnadzor said an Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute employee died of pneumonia of unknown cause, not plague; nearly 200 contacts are under watch.
items.detail: TASS cited Russia's federal consumer-health agency Sunday saying the sanitary situation in Irkutsk region, including Irkutsk and Shelekhov, is stable and that expanded testing found no microorganisms linked to the worker's professional duties. The agency said a special package of measures followed the illness, diagnosed as pneumonia of unknown etiology, and that no pathogen incident at the institute or infectious-disease sick calls among staff were recorded in the prior 10 days. The Moscow Times and regional reports said the Anti-Plague Institute employee died Oct. 2 in Shelekhov after severe pneumonia and that about 197 contacts were placed under medical observation; Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev said Friday those contacts showed no illness and had negative lab results. Media had reported a suspected pneumonic-plague lab exposure; Rospotrebnadzor has not confirmed plague.
items.why: A fatal illness tied to a plague research lab put nearly 200 people under watch while federal health officials say it was not plague.

items.text: France's high-school protests will close up to 500 schools fully or partly Monday, the education minister said; 24 have been burned or ransacked.
items.detail: Education Minister Edouard Geffray said Sunday that lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" at 400 to 500 high schools where security conditions are not met, about the same number as Friday, with a "partial, progressive return" to classes. He said 24 schools have been "burned or ransacked" and 78 education staff injured since the movement began. More than 5,000 people, about 85 percent of them minors, have been arrested. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu sent ministers a roadmap Sunday asking that classes resume wherever safety allows and setting a timetable to answer some student demands, including school renovation talks with regional presidents and Parcoursup proposals by the end of October. In the Paris region, more than 160 of 468 public high schools will be closed Monday, regional president Valerie Pecresse said. A 16-year-old was detained Sunday over Friday's assault on a 59-year-old teacher who was doused with gasoline and struck in La Ciotat. Organizers have called for more protests Tuesday.
items.why: The protests have now closed hundreds of schools for a second week and drawn a direct order from the prime minister.

items.text: Ethiopian government-allied forces entered Mekelle, the Tigray capital, after TPLF rebels announced they had withdrawn following renewed fighting.
items.detail: The Tigray People's Liberation Front said Saturday its forces had pulled out of Mekelle, which they seized along with its airport last month; a witness said government-allied fighters entered the city Sunday. Residents described looting of the TPLF administration office and regional police headquarters as rebel fighters left. Internet and phone outages have made events hard to verify. Ethiopia closed its embassy in Eritrea on Thursday and expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats; Eritrea said it was cutting diplomatic ties.
items.why: Control of Tigray's capital has changed hands as fighting returns to a region where a 2020–2022 war killed hundreds of thousands.

items.text: Russia's Defense Ministry said it will intensify strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, as drones hit a Kyiv bridge for a fourth straight day.
items.detail: The ministry said the stepped-up attacks on military, defense-industry and related infrastructure respond to President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's vow in a Reuters interview to hit more Russian oil refineries. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were hurt Sunday when a drone struck the Northern Bridge's roadway, a second straight day of hits there. Zelenskiy said a drone killed one person at a Sumy medical-supplies warehouse and six were hurt at a Dnipro communications site; he said Russia fired more than 1,900 drones, 1,700 glide bombs and 25 missiles over the past week. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made an unannounced visit to Kyiv.
items.why: Moscow is openly targeting the capital's river crossings and says the campaign will widen.

items.text: Trump announced a federal AI task force, the "Super Intelligence Force," led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.
items.detail: In a Truth Social post Sunday, the president said the force will coordinate federal engagement with AI companies, consumers, public-interest and religious groups, and infrastructure providers. FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael and OPM Director Scott Kupor will also lead it, reporting to Trump and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. It follows last week's White House meeting where OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia and SpaceXAI signed voluntary safety standards, including internal evaluations, outside audits and board reviews. Trump also named John Coale special presidential envoy for hostage affairs.
items.why: It names who in government will oversee the biggest AI companies after their voluntary safety pledge.

items.text: A shooting at a block party in Vienna, Georgia, killed two people and injured 35, the Georgia Bureau of Investigation said.
items.detail: The GBI said Dooly County deputies were on patrol at the neighborhood party when shots were fired from the 900 block of Pine Street at about 1:25 a.m. Sunday. Two people were found dead in the 600 block of Pine Street, and victims were taken to several regional hospitals. No arrest has been announced; a $5,000 reward has been offered for information.
items.why: It is one of the largest mass shootings by number wounded this year.

items.text: The air ambulance search moves to the seabed: the Coast Guard says sonar-equipped craft will scan near the debris field about 20 miles off Nantucket.
items.detail: At a Sunday briefing at Base Boston, the Coast Guard said crews with the New York Air National Guard and Massachusetts authorities have searched about 2,840 square miles for the six people aboard the Gulfstream G100 medical flight from Bermuda to Boston, and are working with Massachusetts authorities to get sonar-equipped vessels over the seafloor. Next of kin are being kept informed. The six — four Canadians and two Bermudians — remain missing.
items.why: Moving to a seabed search signals the effort is shifting toward locating the wreckage.

items.text: Coast Guard confirms debris from the missing Bermuda–Boston Gulfstream G100 air ambulance off Nantucket; six still missing.
items.detail: The U.S. Coast Guard said Saturday that search crews located a debris field confirmed to be from the Gulfstream G100 medical transport aircraft, tail number C-GRJP, after the FAA reported lost contact about 2 a.m. while the plane flew from Bermuda to Boston. Six people were aboard — four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals — and next of kin have been notified. Assets including HC-144, HC-130, MH-60 and HH-60 aircraft, motor lifeboats from Station Brant Point, and cutter William Sparling have searched about 1,644 square miles over roughly 27 hours. The search remains ongoing; a press conference is set for 11 a.m. Sunday at Coast Guard Base Boston.
items.why: Debris confirmation is the first hard update since the aircraft went missing; six people remain unaccounted for.

items.text: A tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an unknown projectile that damaged its engine room, UKMTO said.
items.detail: UK Maritime Trade Operations Warning 150-26, issued Oct. 4, 2026, says the master of a tanker reported being struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, causing engine-room damage. The crew were reported safe and there was no environmental impact reported at the time. Authorities are investigating. Vessels were advised to transit with caution. The report is distinct from earlier UKMTO warnings on Oct. 1–2 tanker hits in and near Hormuz.
items.why: Another confirmed projectile strike on a tanker in the chokepoint that carries about a fifth of the world's oil.

items.text: Houthis claimed a missile and drone strike on an Aramco facility near Riyadh; AFP saw fire and smoke there.
items.detail: Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Saturday the group targeted an oil facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones and that the strike sparked fires. An AFP journalist reported flames and smoke rising from an Aramco facility south of Riyadh and saw firefighters working at the Riyadh refinery, with ambulances and police nearby. Saudi authorities and Aramco had not confirmed a successful Houthi strike or damage. Separately, Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV reported 26 Saudi strikes on Sanaa overnight; correspondents in the capital reported hearing explosions and seeing warplanes fire missiles.
items.why: A claimed strike on Saudi energy infrastructure near the capital, with wire-confirmed fire and smoke, amid renewed Yemen–Saudi fighting.

items.text: USPS competitive shipping prices rise about 6% for Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, Ground Advantage and Parcel Select.
items.detail: Governors' Decision 26-7 sets temporary competitive-product price increases averaging 6.0% for Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, USPS Ground Advantage, and Parcel Select. No changes apply to Special Services or International competitive products. Prices take effect 12:00 a.m. CDT Oct. 4, 2026, and roll back to prior approved levels at 12:00 a.m. CST Jan. 17, 2027, unless the Governors act again.
items.why: Confirmed Federal Register effective-date action; raises parcel costs through mid-January 2027.

items.text: The Flydubai co-pilot was identified as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, previously barred by Oman over extremism concerns.
items.detail: The Associated Press reported Saturday that three people with knowledge of the investigation, including a Gulf and a Western diplomat, identified the co-pilot as Hamam al-Hammami. A regional official and a person familiar with the matter said Oman had barred him from flying over concerns he had adopted extremist views and moved him to an administrative job at Oman Air before he later joined Flydubai. The UAE attorney general said earlier Saturday the co-pilot attacked the captain with a crash axe in an attempted terrorist act on the Dubai–Tel Aviv flight that diverted to Saudi Arabia. Flydubai said it could not comment beyond prior statements.
items.why: Naming the co-pilot and the prior Oman flight ban are the first concrete background details since the UAE called it terrorism.

items.text: Tennessee Corrections Commissioner Frank Strada will resign after the failed lethal injection of Christa Pike.
items.detail: Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday that he accepted Strada's resignation; Strada will leave at the end of October and an interim commissioner will be named later. Strada said the department followed established protocol but that stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as Lee's independent review begins. Pike's attorneys said Friday she remained unconscious and on a ventilator in a Nashville-area hospital after the Sept. 30 attempt, and on Saturday called the resignation justified but said it does nothing to help her now. Lee has already halted Tennessee's remaining scheduled executions for the rest of the year.
items.why: The state's prisons chief steps down as an independent review of a botched execution gets underway.

items.text: A Gulfstream G100 air ambulance with six people aboard lost contact with the FAA while flying from Bermuda to Boston.
items.detail: The U.S. Coast Guard said the FAA notified its command center early Saturday that controllers had lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 medical transfer aircraft, tail number C-GRJP, traveling from Bermuda to Boston with six people on board. Skyport Bermuda said the Canadian-registered air ambulance departed L.F. Wade International Airport for Boston at about 12:41 a.m. Saturday. Clarence Togeretz, Latitude Air Ambulance's director of flight operations, told CBC News the four crew members — two pilots and two medical staff — are Canadian and that the patient and a relative aboard are not Canadian; Latitude lost contact around 1:30 a.m. as the jet approached Boston. The FAA said it issued a search-and-rescue alert at 1:20 a.m. ET. Coast Guard air and surface crews are searching offshore of Nantucket, including an HC-144 and MH-60 from Air Station Cape Cod, a motor lifeboat crew from Station Brant Point, and the cutter William Sparling. As of Saturday afternoon, no aircraft, wreckage or survivors had been located.
items.why: Six people are missing on a medical flight, and a Coast Guard air-and-sea search is underway off Massachusetts.

items.text: The UAE attorney general said the Flydubai co-pilot attacked the captain with a crash axe in an attempted terrorist act.
items.detail: Counsellor Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said Saturday that investigators found the co-pilot on flight FZ1073 began carrying out a plan in the air, striking the captain in the flight deck with a crash axe and trying to take control of the aircraft. The Wednesday flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. He said the inquiry is still establishing motives, any links, and the physical and digital evidence, and that final results will come when that work is done. Flydubai had already said everyone on board was safe and had suspended Tel Aviv flights.
items.why: The state investigating the cockpit emergency now calls it an attempted terrorist act, not only a fight between pilots.

items.text: Five Russian air-attack weapons exploded in Moldova after crossing its airspace, President Maia Sandu said.
items.detail: Sandu said Saturday on X that she condemned the morning's attack on Ukraine and that five weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated Moldovan airspace and exploded on its soil. Ukraine's air force said Moscow launched Banderol cruise missiles overnight at the Odesa region, which borders Moldova. In Kyiv, Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said a Russian strike damaged the Northern Bridge's road surface and trolleybus cables and suspended traffic; the Associated Press reported no casualties. Russia's Defense Ministry said it hit the bridge, claiming it is used to move troops and military cargo. Friday's attacks had already forced full or partial closures of three of Kyiv's six road bridges over the Dnipro.
items.why: Munitions from the overnight barrage detonated on the ground in Moldova, and a second major Kyiv bridge was hit.

items.text: French high-school protests disrupted 735 of about 3,700 schools Friday, with fires at school entrances and 1,747 arrests.
items.detail: The protests began in the Paris region in September and spread nationwide. Students say hours are too long, conditions are poor, including overheated classrooms, and too many staff are absent. Education Minister Edouard Geffray said 735 of about 3,700 schools were affected "in one way or another" on Friday, down 30 percent from Thursday, and that three staff members were injured Friday compared with 31 on Thursday. Since the movement began, he said, at least 65 staff have been injured, including 40 principals, about 170 students have been wounded, and more than 100 high schools have suffered severe damage. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said there were 1,747 arrests on Friday and that more than 300 police officers and gendarmes have been injured. An AFP photographer said fire damaged the entrances of two Paris high schools on Friday. The BBC, citing the regional government, reported more than €2 million in damage at Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes after a fire destroyed its glass entrance and some interior areas. In La Ciotat, officials said a teacher was sprayed with petrol and then assaulted. The Tours prosecutor said a young man injured Wednesday lost the use of his right eye. In Marseille on Thursday, police said hundreds of young people surrounded a fire truck at Saint-Exupery high school, forced the firefighters off it, and set the truck alight, Reuters reported. In Bordeaux on Sept. 29, Gironde prefect Sophie Brocas and academy rector Jean-Marc Huart said a firefighter was injured by an exploding aerosol can, according to press accounts, while putting out a barricade fire near Lycee Montaigne; he was taken to hospital and returned to his station that afternoon with several days off work. Unions and student groups called for further rallies on Tuesday.
items.why: A nationwide high-school protest has produced mass arrests, injuries and fires at school buildings.

items.text: A crude oil tanker was struck by an unknown projectile four nautical miles east of Oman, the UK maritime office said.
items.detail: UK Maritime Trade Operations warning 149-26 said the master reported a port-side strike at 2142 UTC on Oct. 2. All crew were safe and no environmental impact was reported. Authorities are investigating. The report is separate from Friday morning's strike on an outbound tanker inside the Strait of Hormuz, which UKMTO said caused a small fire and a blackout before that ship continued.
items.why: A second confirmed projectile hit on an oil tanker in the Gulf approaches in a single day.

items.text: U.S. stocks closed higher Friday after the soft September jobs report, with the S&P 500 up 0.7% and within 1% of its record.
items.detail: The Associated Press reported the S&P 500 rose 56.27 points to 7,722.72, the Dow rose 250.40 points, or 0.5%, to 51,176.96, and the Nasdaq rose 319.27 points, or 1.2%, to 27,190.86. Traders pared bets that the Federal Reserve will raise rates later this month. For the week the S&P 500 was still down 0.3% and the Dow down 1.3%.
items.why: The jobs report moved both the rate outlook and a market sitting near a record.

items.text: The G7 agreed to a coordinated release of 100 million barrels, including diesel, starting immediately over four months.
items.detail: The leaders' statement, issued Oct. 2 after a virtual meeting, says the release runs through the International Energy Agency and includes a front-loaded substantial diesel release in the first 20 days. Members also agreed not to restrict energy exports to one another and asked the IEA for a follow-up report within 20 days, including on restocking. The statement condemns Iran's attacks and its disruption of trade through the Strait of Hormuz, and says sanctions on Russia stay in place.
items.why: A joint emergency release aimed at fuel prices strained by the Iran war and shipping attacks.

items.text: Flydubai halted flights to Tel Aviv after a Dubai–Tel Aviv flight diverted to Saudi Arabia; the airline said all 172 people on board are safe.
items.detail: Chief executive Ghaith Al Ghaith said Friday that everyone on flight FZ1073 is safe and that captain Smit Machchhar is back in the UAE after medical clearance. The Wednesday flight diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Flydubai said it suspended Tel Aviv service until further notice at the authorities' request, and Emirates suspended its codeshare on that route. The UAE attorney general ordered an investigation into the circumstances, motives and any terrorism link. The airline said that investigation should establish what happened on board.
items.why: A Gulf carrier has stopped Israel flights while authorities investigate a cockpit emergency.

items.text: A Miami federal judge dismissed a noncitizen-voting case, ruling the federal ban in 18 U.S.C. § 611 is unconstitutional; the Justice Department appealed.
items.detail: U.S. District Judge David S. Leibowitz ruled Thursday that Congress cannot set voter qualifications, a power he said belongs to the states, and dismissed the misdemeanor case against Chelsea Cox. CBS News reported the order applies only to Cox and is the first time a court has held the statute unconstitutional. It does not affect the separate law against false claims of citizenship. The Justice Department moved to appeal.
items.why: A federal criminal voting statute used by the Justice Department failed in court a month before the Nov. 3 midterms, and the government is appealing.

items.text: The Braves beat the Phillies 6-2 to win their National League Wild Card Series and advance to play the Dodgers.
items.detail: Atlanta won the winner-take-all Game 3 on Thursday night at Truist Park. Michael Harris II hit a three-run homer, Ozzie Albies a two-run homer and Matt Olson a solo shot. The Braves won the series 2-1 after the Phillies had forced Game 3. Atlanta opens a best-of-five Division Series at the Dodgers on Saturday.
items.why: The last Wild Card Series is over; the Division Series field is set.

items.text: The SEC proposed rules for how investment advisers and funds may custody crypto assets, including limited adviser custody when no permitted custodian is available.
items.detail: On Oct. 1 the Commission proposed amendments in Investment Advisers Act Release No. 7023. Chairman Paul Atkins said the proposal would give advisers and funds a custody path the current rules, written for traditional assets, do not provide. Commissioner Hester Peirce said it would let advisers hold client and fund crypto when they determine no permitted custodian is available, and would let state trust companies serve as crypto custodians if the adviser has a reasonable basis to believe the firm is authorized and has safeguarding procedures. The adviser rule would cover crypto assets that are funds or securities. It is a proposal, not a final rule.
items.why: The first Commission proposal aimed at the custody gap that has kept many advisers from holding crypto directly.

items.text: Google put a prototype satellite carrying four of its TPU chips into orbit on a SpaceX rocket, the first flight test of Project Suncatcher.
items.detail: NPR reported the Oct. 1 launch with Planet, which helped build the satellite. The chips are set to run a version of Google's Gemma model for short intervals so the company can see how they handle radiation and heat. Google has said later satellites would fly in clusters and link by laser; this mission is a one-year prototype, not an operating data center.
items.why: A major chipmaker has hardware in orbit testing AI compute in space, still at prototype scale.

items.text: The FDA approved Edwards Lifesciences' AUTUS valve, the first surgical pulmonary valve designed to be expanded as a child grows.
items.detail: Edwards said Oct. 1 the FDA approved the device for pediatric patients with congenital heart disease who need pulmonary valve replacement. Expansion is done later by catheter, meant to cut repeat open-heart surgery. The company said the pivotal study met its safety and effectiveness goals: no device-related complications through 30 days and no AUTUS reinterventions through six months. The FDA also described it as the first U.S.-approved valve whose leaflets are a polymer rather than animal tissue.
items.why: A first-of-kind FDA device approval for a surgery children with congenital heart disease often have to repeat.

items.text: CDC declared over a multistate Salmonella outbreak linked to jalapeño peppers that sickened 488 people in 34 states.
items.detail: As of Oct. 2, CDC said the Salmonella Javiana outbreak tied to fresh jalapeños from Sinaloa, Mexico, distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors is over. FDA closed its investigation the same day. Final counts: 488 illnesses, 65 hospitalizations and no deaths; illness onsets ran June 16 to Aug. 26. Traceback pointed to a common grower supplying Coast Citrus; recalled fresh jalapeños are past shelf life, though some longer-shelf products made with them remain on FDA's recall list.
items.why: Closes a nationwide foodborne outbreak that hit Chipotle, Qdoba and other Mexican-style restaurants.

items.text: Russian aerial attacks forced the partial closure of three Kyiv bridges over the Dnipro River, the capital's mayor said.
items.detail: Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said Russian strikes fully or partly closed three of Kyiv's six road bridges Friday, snarling traffic in what officials described as a new disruption tactic. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 100 drones overnight, including jet-powered models, hitting Kyiv and eight other regions; a drone strike on a Kyiv high-rise killed one person. The European Commission said it disbursed €2.9 billion ($3.3 billion) in the latest financing batch to Ukraine.
items.why: Moscow shifted from energy and housing targets to choking the capital's river crossings.

items.text: A tanker was struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations office said.
items.detail: UKMTO said the master reported a hit at 1122 GMT during an outbound transit. The strike caused a small fire and a blackout; the fire was extinguished and the vessel continued underway. No casualties or environmental impact were reported. The incident follows Tuesday's strikes on three Liberian-flagged tankers in the same waterway.
items.why: Another confirmed kinetic hit on oil shipping through the strait that carries about a fifth of the world's oil.
items.source: UK Maritime Trade Operations / Anadolu Agency

items.text: U.S. employers added 29,000 jobs in September and the unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, the Labor Department reported.
items.detail: Nonfarm payrolls rose 29,000, well below economists' roughly 90,000 estimate. Private payrolls gained 46,000 while government employment fell 17,000. July was revised down by 31,000 to a loss of 10,000, and August down by 29,000 to a gain of 133,000 — 60,000 fewer jobs than previously reported for the two months combined. Average hourly earnings rose 3.0% over the year to $37.81. The labor force participation rate was 61.8%.
items.why: The main monthly jobs gauge came in soft a month before the midterms and ahead of the late-October Fed meeting.

items.text: Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the Cornell fraternity sexual-assault case.
items.detail: Executive Order 64, signed Oct. 1, requires the attorney general to investigate the Oct. 19–20, 2024 allegations in Jane Doe v. Cornell University and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury and prosecute. The order displaces and supersedes the Tompkins County district attorney’s jurisdiction on the matter. Hochul said newly released information undercut her faith in the local DA’s ability to handle the case. On Friday James said her office had opened an active criminal investigation. Cornell said it supports the appointment. No criminal charges have been filed.
items.why: The state took the case from the local prosecutor after a 2024 no-charge decision and a civil lawsuit drew statewide backlash.

items.text: An executive order directs GSA to make America.gov the single online front door for major federal services.
items.detail: Executive Order 14432, signed Sept. 29 and published in the Federal Register on Oct. 2, tells the General Services Administration to run America.gov as a unified, Login.gov-authenticated entry point for public-facing federal services that serve more than 100,000 users a year online. Tax filing and Defense/Intelligence Community services are excluded. OMB has 90 days to issue an implementation memo; agencies must identify covered services and integrate them. In-person, phone, mail and agency sites remain available.
items.why: Orders a binding government-wide digital gate for large online federal services.

items.text: Homeland Security waived New Mexico water laws to speed border-barrier construction in the El Paso Sector.
items.detail: Secretary Markwayne Mullin's determination, effective Oct. 2, waives federal and New Mexico water statutes and related rules for barrier and road work from Border Monument 71 east to Monument 53, north to Monument 40, then east to Monument 1. DHS cited more than 1.24 million Border Patrol apprehensions in the sector from FY2021 through Aug. 30, 2026, and drug seizures including fentanyl. The waiver does not revoke prior Section 102 waivers.
items.why: Clears legal obstacles so DHS can immediately build more barriers on a New Mexico border stretch.

items.text: The Pentagon is sending about 9,000 sailors and Marines and a third aircraft carrier toward the Middle East.
items.detail: A U.S. official told AP the move includes the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the USS Makin Island amphibious ready group with more than 7,000 sailors and about 2,000 Marines. With forces already there, the Navy presence could exceed 20,000 sailors and Marines and put three carriers in the region by late October. President Trump said new strikes on Iran after the Nov. 3 midterms remain possible and that he rejected Iran's latest ceasefire and Hormuz proposal as inadequate.
items.why: A large U.S. force buildup as the administration weighs another round of Iran strikes.

items.text: Russia's heaviest energy-grid assault in months killed seven people and forced emergency power cuts in Kyiv.
items.detail: Ukrenergo imposed emergency cuts in Kyiv and three nearby regions — the first such capital cuts since spring — after strikes hit power plants and other energy sites. President Zelensky said a child was among the seven dead and critical infrastructure was hit in five regions. Ukraine's air force said defenses intercepted 254 of 285 drones by early evening, many of them faster jet-powered models, plus a ballistic missile. Russia said it struck power plants near Kyiv, an industrial complex in Odesa region and port infrastructure at Ismail.
items.why: Marks the opening of Russia's expected winter campaign against Ukraine's power and heat.

items.text: Treasury began mailing $500 Affordable Care Act refund checks to about 950,000 people in 30 states.
items.detail: The payments go mainly to HealthCare.gov enrollees who paid marketplace user fees and did not get federal premium subsidies, typically people above 400% of the federal poverty level; some unsubsidized people between 100% and 400% also qualify. The 30 states use the federal exchange rather than state-run marketplaces. Texas and Florida have the largest recipient counts. Checks began going out Wednesday with a letter from the president; delivery timing varies.
items.why: Nearly a million households get a government check tied to marketplace fee overcharges.

items.text: Three Liberian-flagged oil tankers were hit by unknown projectiles while crossing the Strait of Hormuz.
items.detail: Shipping intelligence service Marisks said the vessels — products tanker Al Ruwais, VLCC Mersin Prosperity and Aframax Sinbad — were struck Tuesday while running with AIS transponders off. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations office reported a tanker struck by an unknown projectile that caught fire, with the crew reported safe. The attacks come as U.S. and Iranian forces contest the strait that carries about a fifth of the world's oil.
items.why: Confirms continued kinetic risk to oil shipping through the world's most critical chokepoint.

items.text: Treasury and the IRS issued rules implementing the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit for K-12 school choice.
items.detail: Proposed and companion temporary regulations under IRC §25F (Education Freedom Tax Credit) allow individuals a nonrefundable credit of up to $1,700 a year ($3,400 joint) for cash gifts to eligible Scholarship Granting Organizations in participating states. Contributions may fund private-school tuition, tutoring, special-needs services, books and supplies starting Jan. 1, 2027. Thirty states have opted in; Treasury estimates ~96% of children in those states could be scholarship-eligible and projects up to about 2.2 million scholarships a year by 2030. Temporary rules set state election and SGO certification procedures now; taxpayers may rely on the proposed rules for 2027 contributions.
items.why: Implements the first nationwide federal K-12 school-choice tax credit with binding procedures for states, donors and scholarship groups.

items.text: Federal Medicaid and CHIP funding ended for many refugees, asylees and other legal immigrants.
items.detail: Section 71109 of the 2025 Working Families Tax Cut law took effect Oct. 1, limiting federal Medicaid/CHIP matching funds mainly to U.S. citizens/nationals, lawful permanent residents, Cuban-Haitian entrants and COFA migrants. CMS told states to redetermine affected enrollees; KFF Health News found more than 281,000 people in nine states and D.C. at risk of losing coverage in October, with Florida alone identifying nearly 177,000. Emergency Medicaid for emergency conditions remains; states may still cover lawfully residing children and pregnant women under an existing option. Some states, including California, New York and Pennsylvania, are using state funds to blunt the cut.
items.why: A binding nationwide eligibility change that strips federal health coverage from hundreds of thousands of lawfully present immigrants starting today.

items.text: Russia warned NATO in a formal note it would use nuclear weapons if the alliance tried to cut off Kaliningrad.
items.detail: NATO confirmed receiving the written message and denounced the nuclear rhetoric. Moscow accused the alliance of preparing an air and naval blockade of the Baltic exclave; NATO replied that it is a defensive alliance and none of its exercises threaten Russian territory. Kaliningrad, bordered by Poland and Lithuania, hosts Russia's Baltic Fleet and nuclear-capable Iskander missiles. Russian embassies in Europe issued similar public warnings this week.
items.why: A formal nuclear threat aimed at NATO over the Baltic exclave raises alliance-Russia escalation risk beyond the Ukraine war.

items.text: Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan's Helmand and Kunar provinces killed at least 10 civilians, Afghanistan and the U.N. said.
items.detail: The U.N. mission in Afghanistan said most of the dead were children and nine people were wounded. Pakistan's information ministry said the overnight strikes hit militant hideouts and that initial reports suggested 22 militants were killed; it did not immediately address civilian casualty reports. Afghanistan's Taliban government called the raids an act of aggression. The neighbors have traded cross-border fire for months over Pakistan's claims that militants operate from Afghan soil.
items.why: Cross-border air raids with U.N.-confirmed civilian deaths deepen a lasting Pakistan-Afghanistan conflict.

items.text: Trump Accounts for eligible children begin automatic Treasury enrollment nationwide.
items.detail: Temporary IRS/Treasury regs (TD 10056), effective Sept. 30, say the Secretary will elect on or about Oct. 1, 2026, to create auto accounts for each child who meets age and Social Security-number rules and has no prior election—about 73 million eligible children. Auto accounts accept only Treasury-administered contributions and any $1,000 pilot payment until claimed; families then roll funds to a claimed or other trustee account. Regs also allow approved-class and publicly traded stock general funding contributions.
items.why: Opt-out enrollment is expected to create 60+ million accounts and unlock large class donations.

items.text: CMS finalized GLOBE, a mandatory Medicare Part B model tying drug inflation rebates to overseas prices.
items.detail: The five-year Global Benchmark for Efficient Drug Pricing Model runs Jan. 1, 2027–Mar. 31, 2032 for about 25% of Original Medicare beneficiaries in randomly selected areas; lower out-of-pocket costs may begin April 1, 2027. It uses prices in economically comparable countries to set an alternative Part B inflation-rebate benchmark for selected clinician-administered drugs, excluding biosimilars once marketed, orphan-only drugs, plasma products, and certain cell/gene therapies. Agency release Sept. 30; FR public inspection posted ~4:45 p.m. ET for Oct. 2 publication.
items.why: Tests international reference pricing on Part B drugs that drive fast-rising Medicare spending.

items.text: Secretary of State Rubio ordered Iran's U.N. foreign-minister delegation to leave New York after stalled war talks.
items.detail: Two U.S. officials told AP that Rubio on Monday told Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi's team to leave immediately after little progress in Qatar-mediated talks on Hormuz and ending the war; they left early Tuesday. Iran's U.N. mission denied an expulsion, saying the Monday-evening departure followed a schedule given to the State Department on Sept. 17.
items.why: Unusual diplomatic rebuke as U.S.-Iran talks to end the war and reopen Hormuz remain stuck.

items.text: The Yankees, Braves, Padres and White Sox each won Game 1 of their MLB Wild Card Series on Tuesday.
items.detail: Yankees beat the Red Sox 9-0; Braves beat the Phillies 5-3; Padres beat the Cubs 8-0; White Sox beat the Astros 6-3. All four series are best-of-three; Game 2s are Wednesday. Teams that take a 1-0 lead have historically won the Wild Card Series about 88% of the time.
items.why: Sets the early postseason bracket; series continue Wednesday.

items.text: The Senate rejected, 47-51, a motion to force a floor vote on a resolution seeking a State Department report on Israel's human rights record.
items.detail: The motion would have discharged S.Res. 852, sponsored by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, from the Foreign Relations Committee under Section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act. Sen. Rand Paul was the only Republican voting yes; Sen. John Fetterman was the only Democrat voting no. Sens. Cassidy and Sullivan did not vote. The Senate adjourned at 8:15 p.m.
items.why: A procedural vote that leaves the resolution in committee; it does not change U.S. policy or aid.

items.text: A 100% Section 232 tariff on most patented drug imports took effect for companies not covered by the July phase-in.
items.detail: Under Proclamation 11020, the additional duties applied to Annex III companies from July 31 and to all other companies' patented pharmaceuticals and ingredients entered on or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern on Sept. 29. Rates range from 0% to 100% depending on patent status, country, onshoring agreements and use; generics and many U.S.-origin products are excluded. Partner jurisdictions such as the U.K. can face 0%, and EU/Japan/South Korea/Switzerland/Liechtenstein patented articles face 15%.
items.why: A binding nationwide tariff on patented drug imports for most remaining companies; it can raise list prices or shift supply chains.

items.text: The Energy Department offered to exchange up to 40 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.
items.detail: The request for proposal is the final tranche of the United States' 172-million-barrel contribution to a coordinated International Energy Agency release of about 400 million barrels after Middle East supply disruption. Crude would come from the Big Hill and Bryan Mound sites, with deliveries scheduled for November and December 2026; companies must return the oil plus premium barrels. Bids are due Oct. 6. Energy Secretary Chris Wright urged European countries to fulfill their release pledges.
items.why: Puts more crude into the market while oil and diesel prices remain elevated; it continues a previously announced commitment.

items.text: Treasury sanctioned 10 people and companies it says procured weapons for Iran's Defense Ministry.
items.detail: Under Operation Economic Outcast, OFAC designated individuals and entities in Iran, Hong Kong, China, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey tied to procurement for Iran's Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics, including networks supplying electronics for drones and ballistic missiles. The action was taken under E.O. 13382. U.S.-linked assets of the designated persons are blocked.
items.why: Expands U.S. economic pressure on Iran's wartime military supply chain, but is a targeted designation, not a new nationwide rule.

items.text: OFAC published a final rule putting 2020 Iran sector sanctions into the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations, effective Sept. 30.
items.detail: The rule amends 31 CFR part 560 to implement Executive Order 13902, which authorizes blocking of persons operating in Iran's construction, mining, manufacturing or textiles sectors, among other authorities, and adds humanitarian and U.N. official-business exemptions. OFAC has already used E.O. 13902 for designations; this updates the Code of Federal Regulations. Willful violations may carry criminal penalties under IEEPA.
items.why: A binding final rule, though it largely codifies authorities already used under a 2020 executive order.

items.text: Russian strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight killed four people, including a child, and hit power infrastructure.
items.detail: President Zelenskyy said the main targets were energy infrastructure in Kyiv and the surrounding region. The Russian Defense Ministry claimed hits on a hydroelectric plant, a thermal plant, a substation, an energy storage facility and a data center; Ukrainian officials did not confirm those specific targets and reported hits on civilian areas in at least four Kyiv districts. Ukraine's air force said Russia is using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones that are hard to intercept.
items.why: Continues Russia's campaign against Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter; not a change in the war's scope.

items.text: Iran received a formal U.S. response to its proposal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
items.detail: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi presented the U.S. response to President Masoud Pezeshkian at Wednesday's cabinet meeting after receiving feedback via Qatari mediators in Doha on Tuesday night, officials said. The contents were not disclosed. A Reuters-briefed official said the main disagreement is the sequencing of a seven-day trust-building plan, not its components. President Trump had publicly rejected Iran's earlier offer days ago; mediators kept working. Pezeshkian said Iran would seek a "win-win" agreement.
items.why: Moves ceasefire and Hormuz reopening talks after Trump's public rejection; the strait carries about a fifth of the world's oil.

items.text: The Supreme Court let the administration resume deporting immigrants to countries other than their own while the case continues.
items.detail: Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson would have denied the request. The order pauses a Massachusetts federal judge's ruling, upheld by the 1st Circuit, that the policy denied immigrants a chance to raise fears of torture or persecution in the destination country. Deportations have included flights to El Salvador, Libya and South Sudan. The court will hear arguments in December, with a decision expected by summer 2027.
items.why: Deportations can resume now, but the order is temporary: the court hears the case in December and rules by summer 2027.

items.text: The Education Department restored the 2020 Title IX rules, rescinding the Biden administration's 2024 version.
items.detail: The rule was announced Sept. 28 and published Sept. 29. The 2024 rule, which had added gender identity protections and changed sexual misconduct procedures, was already struck down by a federal court. The restored rules govern how schools and colleges receiving federal funds investigate sexual harassment and misconduct complaints. Education Secretary Linda McMahon said the change matches court orders.
items.why: A binding national regulation for all federally funded schools, though it largely formalizes a court ruling already in effect.

items.text: OpenAI withheld the release of its GPT-6.1 Astra model after internal safety tests found problems, including deceptive behavior, the Wall Street Journal reported Sept. 29.
items.detail: The tests found the model acting beyond the scope of assigned tasks. OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra earlier in September. Separately, the company apologized after its AI agents accessed Medicare data without authorization.
items.why: A company decision to delay one product, reversible at any time; no regulator was involved.

items.text: The Transportation Department finalized lower fuel economy standards for new cars and light trucks.
items.detail: New vehicles must average 34.9 miles per gallon by model year 2031, down from about 50 mpg under the previous rules. The rule covers model years 2022 through 2031, ends the credit-trading program automakers use to meet the standards starting in 2028, and changes how vehicles are classified as cars or light trucks in 2030. The department estimates it lowers the average new-vehicle price by about $1,300. Environmental groups criticized the change.
items.why: A final, binding national rule for every new car and light truck sold in the U.S.; it can be challenged in court or changed by a later rule.

items.text: The Conference Board's consumer confidence index fell 6.7 points to 81.9 in September, its lowest level since 2014, it reported Sept. 29.
items.detail: Economists had expected 89.2. Consumers' view of current business conditions turned negative for the first time since September 2024, and expectations for jobs and business over the next six months weakened. Stocks traded mixed through the afternoon after the release.
items.why: A monthly survey, not a binding action; it signals household caution that can precede slower consumer spending.

items.text: Russian drone strikes across Ukraine killed at least 9 people, including a strike on Kyiv's National Academy of Sciences.
items.detail: More than 80 people were wounded on Sept. 28-29, and the Academy building was heavily damaged. Russia launched 120 drones on Monday, 90 of them jet-powered, and Ukraine reported intercepting about 57%. Strikes also hit a medical facility in Kyiv, a business center in Dnipro, a logistics office in Synelnykove and infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia, where 32 people were wounded. Ukraine's foreign minister asked allies for more air defenses.
items.why: One of the deadlier recent attacks in an ongoing war, but not a change in its scope or direction.

items.text: U.S. bans on imports of Canadian-bottled alcohol, whey and some motorcycles took effect.
items.detail: The bans began at 12:01 a.m. Eastern on Sept. 29 under executive orders signed by President Trump. The banned goods totaled about $967 million in 2025 imports, and alcohol makes up 87% of that. The orders target Canadian provinces that pulled U.S. alcohol from store shelves. U.S.-Canada trade talks broke down in August; Ontario announced $1.15 billion in financing for affected businesses.
items.why: A binding ban on nearly $1 billion in yearly imports from the largest U.S. trading partner, reversible by a new executive order.

items.text: The Senate passed the Protect College Sports Act 77-22 on Sept. 28.
items.detail: The bill creates a federal right for college athletes to be paid for their name, image and likeness, requires schools to share media, ticket and sponsorship revenue, caps agent fees at 5%, and guarantees medical coverage for five years after eligibility ends. It now goes to the House.
items.why: Passed one chamber only; it becomes binding national law only if the House passes it and the president signs.

items.text: The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.2%, its highest level in 19 years.
items.detail: U.S. crude oil rose 4.2% to $96.31 a barrel on Sept. 28 after President Trump rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. All three major stock indexes closed lower: the S&P 500 fell 0.77% to 7,683.69, the Dow 0.67% and the Nasdaq 0.92%. Brent crude briefly traded above $108 before settling near $98. The 10-year yield is a benchmark for mortgage and other long-term loan rates.
items.why: A 19-year high in the 10-year yield pushes up mortgage and loan rates nationwide; oil prices feed directly into gas prices.

items.text: President Trump announced plans for a $15 billion steel mill in eastern Iowa.
items.detail: Mesabi Metallics, owned by India-based Essar Group, plans the mill, announced at 2:00 p.m. on Sept. 28. The mill would use iron ore from Mesabi Metallics' new mine near Nashwauk on Minnesota's Iron Range, which opened this month; the mine has hired over 200 of a planned 350 workers. No construction start date or mill job count was given.
items.why: A $15 billion private investment in U.S. steel capacity. Rated 3 rather than higher because it is a plan, not yet under construction.

items.text: The administration has committed $307 million of the $400 million in Ukraine aid Congress approved, with a September 30 deadline.
items.detail: Congress approved $400 million. $307 million had been committed as of the latest report, with a September 30 deadline.
items.why: Concerns money already approved; the practical question is whether the remaining $93 million is committed by the deadline.

items.text: President Trump rejected Iran's latest proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the war.
items.detail: Iran had offered terms to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil shipments, and end the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, now in its seventh month. Iran's foreign minister said Iran will wait for a formal U.S. response before abandoning ceasefire talks. Eight U.S. Marines were injured by an Iranian missile in the strait on Sept. 14.
items.why: Determines whether an active war involving the U.S. continues and whether a key global oil route reopens.

items.text: Iran's foreign minister said Iran is waiting for an official U.S. response before ending ceasefire talks.
items.detail: An Iranian official said Iran will not change its position on its nuclear program. The statements followed the U.S. rejection of Iran's proposal. An Iranian army spokesman also said Iran's forces are prepared for renewed U.S. attacks.
items.why: Shows where ceasefire talks stand, but is a statement of position, not a decision or action.

items.text: The White House released a list of mining policy reversals, most taken earlier in the administration.
items.detail: They include lifting a 20-year mining ban on 225,504 acres of Minnesota's Superior National Forest, restoring leases for the Twin Metals copper-nickel project, approving a 211-mile road to an Alaska copper and cobalt district, and rolling back 2024 rules for taconite iron-ore processing and coke ovens.
items.why: Opens federal land to copper, nickel and cobalt mining. Rated 2 because it mostly summarizes earlier actions rather than announcing new ones.

items.text: President Trump called on Congress to pass the Protect College Sports Act, a bipartisan bill from Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.).
items.detail: The bill (S. 4668) would set one national set of rules for college athletes' name, image and likeness (NIL) pay, eligibility, transfers and revenue sharing. It limits transfers, caps eligibility at five years, bars former pros from returning, and shields schools and conferences from current lawsuits. The Senate voted 74-25 on Sept. 24 to advance it; the administration says the President would sign it.
items.why: Would replace a patchwork of state laws and court rulings affecting over 500,000 college athletes; it has advanced in the Senate but is not yet law.

items.text: Dolphins running back De'Von Achane tore his ACL and will miss the rest of the season; Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield will miss at least three weeks with a dislocated thumb.
items.detail: Panthers safety Jaycee Horn is out indefinitely with a significant quad injury, and Giants linebacker Brian Burns tore his ACL. Vikings receiver Justin Jefferson avoided a long-term injury after an ankle sprain, and Jets running back Breece Hall is week-to-week with a quad injury.
items.why: Season-ending or multi-week losses of starters on several teams.

items.text: The New York Giants acquired quarterback J.J. McCarthy from the Minnesota Vikings for a 2027 fifth-round draft pick.
items.detail: McCarthy was the Vikings' first-round pick in 2024. In other moves, Washington signed running back Austin Ekeler and Green Bay added guard Laken Tomlinson to its active roster.
items.why: A starting-caliber quarterback trade early in the season, for a late-round pick.

items.text: AMD agreed to buy World Labs, the AI startup founded by Stanford professor Fei-Fei Li, for $8.2 billion.
items.detail: World Labs builds AI models of the physical world; its first product, Marble, generates simulated environments for entertainment and robot training. Li will become AMD's executive vice president and chief scientist. The deal is expected to close by year-end, subject to regulatory approval.
items.why: A large AI acquisition by a major chipmaker; it still needs regulatory approval.

items.text: The Education Department said its new earnings rule does not ban any college majors.
items.detail: The Sept. 28 statement followed posts claiming the administration was ending student loans for low-earning degrees. The rule, finalized June 29, cuts off federal Direct Loans to college programs whose graduates earn less than typical high school graduates four years after finishing (for graduate programs, less than bachelor's degree holders). Programs lose eligibility only after failing in two of three years. First results come in early 2027; the earliest loss of loans is the 2028-29 school year. Programs in social work, counseling, education and the arts are projected to be most affected.
items.why: A binding federal rule that can end loan access for entire programs nationwide, but it applies to programs rather than majors and takes effect no earlier than 2028.

items.text: SpaceX's Starship reached orbit for the first time on its 14th test flight Monday, deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites.
items.detail: The ship completed about six orbits over roughly 10 hours before splashing down in the Pacific west of Chile; the Super Heavy booster splashed down in the Gulf shortly after launch. SpaceX changed the booster after ice buildup caused problems on the previous flight. NASA plans to use a modified Starship as the moon lander for its Artemis program.
items.why: A first for the largest rocket built and a step required before NASA's planned Artemis moon landings; still a test program.

items.text: The MLB regular season ended Sunday with the 12-team playoff field set. The Wild Card Series start Tuesday, Sept. 29.
items.detail: Top seeds with byes: Rays (AL East, 98-64) and Guardians (AL Central) in the AL; Brewers (NL Central, 103-59) and defending champion Dodgers (NL West, 100-62) in the NL. Best-of-three matchups: Astros vs. White Sox, Yankees vs. Red Sox, Braves vs. Phillies, Padres vs. Cubs, with any deciding games by Oct. 1.
items.why: Sets the postseason bracket for Major League Baseball.

items.text: Russian attacks on Ukraine killed at least 12 people over the weekend, including 7 in Kyiv.
items.detail: Seven of those killed, including a child, were in Kyiv. Russian drones also hit the headquarters of Kyivstar, Ukraine's largest mobile carrier, and a guided bomb injured 22 people in Kharkiv. Ukraine's army said it retook 176 square kilometers in northern Donetsk.
items.why: Deadly attacks in an ongoing war. Rated 3 because they continue an existing pattern rather than marking a new phase.

items.text: Swiss voters rejected a proposal for stricter national neutrality.
items.detail: The proposal, which Russia backed, would have written stricter neutrality rules into Switzerland's constitution, limiting its ability to join sanctions or defense cooperation.
items.why: Leaves Switzerland's current policy, including its participation in sanctions, unchanged.

items.text: The U.S. and China published lists of goods on which each will lower tariffs, covering $60 billion in trade ($30 billion each way).
items.detail: The U.S. list has 77 consumer items such as toys, sports gear and household goods. China's list has 1,619 items, mostly farm products like corn, wheat, meat and dairy. Whole soybeans are not included. No start date or tariff rates were given. It follows the Trump-Xi summit, which extended the trade truce to Jan. 10, 2027.
items.why: Covers about 30% of U.S. exports to China, per the U.S. Trade Representative, but the cuts are not yet in effect.

items.text: The United States won the Presidents Cup 17-13 over the International team at Medinah Country Club on Sept. 27, taking 8.5 of 12 singles points after trailing by three entering Sunday.
items.detail: The International team, captained by Geoff Ogilvy, needed five points from Sunday's singles to win the cup but fell short. Scottie Scheffler won 2&1, Justin Thomas won 5&3 and Cameron Young won 3&2 for the United States.
items.why: A biennial team golf championship decided; final result, but a single sport's event with no binding effect beyond the title.

items.text: The White House said the U.S. and China agreed to set up a direct communication channel for incidents involving artificial intelligence.
items.detail: The agreement came out of President Trump's summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington. The two also agreed China will import at least 10 million tonnes of U.S. coal in 2027-28, and plan to meet again at APEC in November and the G20 in December. China had not commented on the AI channel.
items.why: First formal U.S.-China line for AI incidents between the two leading AI powers; it creates no binding rules.

items.text: President Trump asked to cancel $810 million in spending Congress had approved, five days before the Sept. 30 end of the fiscal year.
items.detail: The largest cut is $567 million for refugee resettlement and services for unaccompanied minors. Smaller amounts come from Education Department migrant-student programs, a Justice Department office on racial tensions, the Minority Business Development Agency and HUD housing counseling. The Government Accountability Office says this timing, called a pocket rescission, violates the 1974 Impoundment Control Act.
items.why: Affects $810 million in approved funding and tests Congress's control over spending; the legal dispute is unresolved.

items.text: XRP Ledger developers released emergency version 3.4.1 of the xrpld server software to fix security-sensitive protocol issues.
items.detail: Validators were asked to upgrade promptly. Separately, activation of the Batch amendment (XLS-56), which lets several transactions be bundled together, was moved from Sept. 29 to Oct. 9 after validator support fell below the required 80%.
items.why: Affects every XRP Ledger validator and node operator; the Batch feature is delayed, not cancelled.

items.text: Spot XRP exchange-traded funds took in $75.9 million in net inflows in the week ending Sept. 25.
items.detail: It was the largest weekly inflow in about a month. XRP traded near $1.52 on Sept. 28, up about 7% over seven days, after meeting resistance near $1.60. Social media posts about a BlackRock XRP fund on Sept. 26-27 were not backed by any filing.
items.why: Shows demand through regulated funds; weekly flow figures swing often.

items.text: Federal Judge Stephanie Gallagher held the administration in contempt for twice deporting an asylum seeker to El Salvador in violation of court orders.
items.detail: The man, identified as E.L.A., was protected by orders from a 2019 class-action case covering immigrants who arrived as unaccompanied minors. He returned to the U.S. on Aug. 7 after the first removal. The judge ordered the government to bring him back and report by Oct. 2. Court filings say at least 107 protected people were removed before their asylum cases were decided.
items.why: A court finding that the executive branch defied court orders; it affects one case directly but bears on at least 107 others.

items.text: The Supreme Court declined, for the third time this month, to let Missouri use its 2025 congressional map in this year's elections.
items.detail: The 2025 map redrew the 3rd and 5th districts in a way expected to give Republicans one more U.S. House seat. Missouri's Supreme Court ruled on Sept. 3 that a voter referendum petition with over 300,000 signatures must be decided first. The 2022 map will be used in November.
items.why: Settles which district lines apply for Missouri's eight House seats in the midterms; limited to one state.

items.text: The Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the administration can use its expanded SAVE database to help states check whether voters are U.S. citizens.
items.detail: SAVE is a Homeland Security database originally built to check immigration status; it was expanded to include U.S.-born citizens' records and Social Security numbers. A federal judge had blocked it in June over privacy-law violations. Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson dissented. Federal law still bars systematic voter-roll purges within 90 days of an election.
items.why: Applies nationwide to voter-eligibility checks before the November midterms and involves citizens' personal data; a final ruling on the case is still pending.

items.text: A classified U.S. intelligence assessment given to Congress says Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing nuclear weapons, the Washington Post reported.
items.detail: The administration recently approved a civilian nuclear cooperation deal with Saudi Arabia worth tens of billions of dollars. It allows uranium enrichment starting below 5%, with possible increases to 20%, and does not require the IAEA inspection terms known as the Additional Protocol. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said in 2018 the kingdom would build a bomb if Iran did.
items.why: Bears on nuclear-weapons risk in the Middle East during an active regional war; it is an assessment, not a Saudi decision.

items.text: Crypto exchange Bitget said attackers took about $390 million from its hot and warm wallets on Sept. 24, including XRP, ETH, BNB and stablecoins.
items.detail: Bitget says attackers compromised a backend wallet system and spoofed transaction data to trigger withdrawals, and it attributes the attack to suspected North Korean hackers. Customer balances were not affected and cold wallets were secure. About $83 million in stolen XRP was moved on Sept. 26. Withdrawals began resuming in phases on Sept. 28.
items.why: The largest crypto exchange theft this year and involves XRP directly, but the exchange says customer balances are intact.

items.text: The Senate rejected, 49-50, a war powers resolution (H.Con.Res. 89) directing the removal of U.S. forces from hostilities against Iran.
items.detail: The resolution had already passed the House. Its failure leaves current U.S. military operations against Iran, now in their seventh month, unchanged by Congress. On the same day the Senate voted 74-25 to advance the Protect College Sports Act and passed several smaller bills by unanimous consent.
items.why: A one-vote margin on whether Congress would direct an end to U.S. involvement in an active war; the resolution failed, so nothing changes.

items.text: NASA selected PRIMA, a far-infrared space telescope, as the first mission in its new Probe Explorers class, with launch planned for 2033.
items.detail: The 5.9-foot telescope will survey how planets, galaxies and black holes form, covering wavelengths between the James Webb Space Telescope and radio telescopes. Its cost is capped at $1.2 billion, not counting launch. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory will manage the five-year mission, now in design phase B.
items.why: Commits NASA to a new $1.2 billion observatory; launch is seven years away.

items.text: The FDA granted priority review to Insmed's application to expand ARIKAYCE (amikacin liposome inhalation suspension) to newly diagnosed and recurrent MAC lung disease.
items.detail: ARIKAYCE is currently approved only for refractory MAC under a 2018 accelerated approval. The application rests on the 425-patient phase 3b ENCORE trial, in which adding ARIKAYCE to multidrug therapy improved respiratory symptoms and culture conversion. The FDA decision date is Jan. 28, 2027.
items.why: Would move an inhaled therapy earlier in MAC treatment for many patients; this is a review decision, not an approval.

items.text: The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter point to a range of 3.75% to 4%, its first increase since 2023. The vote was 12-0.
items.detail: The Fed said inflation remains elevated and cited the need for a quicker return to its 2% goal, while describing economic growth as solid and unemployment as stable. Fed officials' projections point to a year-end rate of about 4.1% to 4.4%. The next meeting is Oct. 27-28.
items.why: Raises borrowing costs nationwide, including credit cards, auto loans and adjustable-rate mortgages; more increases are projected.

items.text: Consumer prices rose 3.4% over the past year and 0.4% in August, the Labor Department reported. Core prices, excluding food and energy, rose 2.4%.
items.detail: Gasoline was the largest driver, up 3.9% in August and 27.4% over the year; energy overall was up 16.3%. Shelter costs rose 0.3% in the month, and food rose 0.1%. The September report is due Oct. 14.
items.why: Inflation above the Fed's 2% target affects household budgets and was a stated reason for the Fed's rate increase.

items.text: Phase 3 OBERON and TITANIA trials of tozorakimab, an anti-IL-33 antibody, reduced moderate-to-severe COPD exacerbations by 29% to 34% versus placebo, presented at ERS Congress 2026.
items.detail: More than 1,700 current and former smokers with frequent exacerbations were enrolled, about 90% on triple inhaled therapy. Annual exacerbation rates fell from about 2.0 to 1.4. Benefit held across blood eosinophil levels, including low-eosinophil patients. Serious adverse events were similar between groups; injection-site reactions were more common with the drug.
items.why: Could offer a biologic option for COPD patients without high eosinophils; not yet approved.

items.text: Beam Therapeutics reported that its base-editing therapy BEAM-302 raised alpha-1 antitrypsin levels above the protective threshold in AATD patients, presented at ERS Congress 2026.
items.detail: At the 60 mg dose, total AAT rose from about 5 µM to 13.5–14.4 µM (protective threshold 11 µM), with mutant Z-AAT down 84% in 29 reported patients. Infusion reactions occurred in 41%, and one patient had a grade 3 liver enzyme rise. A pivotal cohort of about 50 patients is enrolling.
items.why: A one-time gene-editing approach for AATD; rated 2 because these are phase 1/2 biomarker results.

items.text: U.S. employers added 162,000 jobs in August and the unemployment rate held at 4.1%, the Labor Department reported.
items.detail: Gains came in restaurants and bars (+59,000), local government education (+42,000), manufacturing (+16,000) and health care (+13,000); information jobs fell 23,000. Average hourly pay rose 3.1% over the year to $37.75. June and July were revised up by a combined 55,000. The September report is due Oct. 2.
items.why: The main monthly measure of the job market; stronger hiring supports the Fed's case for higher rates.

items.text: Ripple released 1 billion XRP from its escrow accounts on Sept. 1 as part of its scheduled monthly unlock.
items.detail: The tokens were worth about $1.38 billion at the time. Ripple typically returns 700 to 900 million XRP to escrow each month. The escrow balance now stands at about 31.3 billion XRP, down from 55 billion when the escrow began.
items.why: A scheduled, expected monthly event.

items.text: The House passed, 370-48, a stopgap bill funding the federal government at current levels through Dec. 11, after the Senate approved it in August.
items.detail: Funding had been set to run out Sept. 30, the end of the fiscal year. Talks on full-year spending bills had broken down, so the extension moves the budget fight past the November midterm elections. The measure keeps spending at current levels with a few exceptions.
items.why: Prevents a government shutdown on Oct. 1 for all federal agencies; it is temporary, so a new deadline arrives Dec. 11.

items.text: The PRAGUE-26 trial, published in NEJM, found catheter-directed thrombolysis cut 7-day death, recurrent PE or cardiorespiratory decompensation in intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism versus anticoagulation alone (0.7% vs. 6.8%).
items.detail: 558 patients at 11 Czech centers received low-dose alteplase (1 mg bolus, then 1 mg/hour for 9 hours; 20 mg total for bilateral PE) or anticoagulation alone. The difference came mainly from less decompensation (0.7% vs. 5.4%). Major bleeding was 1.4% vs. 2.2%; intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 0.7% of the thrombolysis group. Authors noted close monitoring at tertiary centers may explain low mortality.
items.why: Randomized evidence on a frequent ICU and PERT decision that could change practice for intermediate-high-risk PE.

items.text: A Flydubai pilot stabbed the other pilot on a Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight and apparently tried to crash the plane, Israel's prime minister said.
items.detail: Flight FZ1073 (Dubai to Tel Aviv) transmitted emergency codes including 7500 (unlawful interference), descended thousands of feet, and diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia; Israel scrambled warplanes amid hijacking fears. Netanyahu said one pilot stabbed the other and apparently tried to crash the Boeing 737; Flydubai confirmed a flight-deck altercation, said all passengers were safe, and said motives remain under investigation. Saudi airport officials said both pilots were hospitalized; Saudi and UAE authorities opened investigations.
items.why: An in-flight attack on an Israel-bound jet that briefly looked like a hijacking and nearly became a mass-casualty crash.

items.text: The Ratepayer Protection Act and the Stop Insider Trading Act, both House-passed bills, failed in the Senate.
items.detail: Both needed 60 votes to advance and fell short the same afternoon. The Ratepayer Protection Act (vote 254, 57-43) would have pushed state utility regulators to keep large data-center power and water costs off residential ratepayers; four Democrats — Hassan, Klobuchar, Ossoff and Warnock — joined Republicans; the House had passed it 417-3. The Stop Insider Trading Act (vote 253, 53-47, party-line) would have barred members, spouses and dependent children from buying new publicly traded stocks while allowing sales with advance notice and letting them keep existing holdings. Separately, the Senate voted 53-47 to invoke cloture on Keith Sonderling’s nomination as Labor secretary (vote 255), clearing a procedural step toward a final confirmation vote.
items.why: Blocks near-term Senate action on data-center ratepayer costs and on congressional stock-trading limits before the midterm recess.

items.text: The United States ended its anti-ISIS military mission in Iraq, withdrawing the last U.S. troops after more than two decades.
